1. ( 1) This Act may be called the Competition Act, 2001.
(2) It extends to the whole of India except the State of
Jammu and Kashmir.
(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central
Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint:
Provided that different dates may be appointed for different
provisions of the Act and any reference in any such provision to the
commencement of this Act shall be construed as a reference to the
coming into force of that provision.
2. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,—
(a) “acquisition” means, directly or indirectly, acquiring or
agreeing to acquire—
(i) shares, voting rights or assets of any enterprise; or
(ii) control over management or control over assets of
any enterprise;

Prohibition of agreements
3. ( 1) No enterprise or association of enterprises or person or
association of persons shall enter into any agreement in respect of
production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods
or provision of services, which causes or is likely to cause an
appreciable adverse effect on competition within India.
(2) Any agreement entered into in contravention of the provisions
contained in sub-section ( 1) shall be void.
(3) Any agreement entered into between enterprises or associations
of enterprises or persons or associations of persons or between any
person and enterprise or practice carried on, or decision taken by, any
association of enterprises or association of persons, including cartels,
engaged in identical or similar trade of goods or provision of services,
which—
(a) directly or indirectly determines purchase or sale
prices;
(b) limits or controls production, supply, markets, technical
development, investment or provision of services;
(c) shares the market or source of production or provision
of services by way of allocation of geographical area of market,
or type of goods or services, or number of customers in the
market or any other similar way;

(d) directly or indirectly results in bid rigging or collusive
bidding, shall be presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect
on competition.
Explanation—For the purposes of this sub-section,—
(a) “bid rigging” means any agreement, between enterprises
or persons referred to in sub-section ( 3) engaged in identical or
similar production or trading of goods or provision of services,
which has the effect of eliminating or reducing competition for
bids or adversely affecting or manipulating the process for
bidding;
(b) “cartel” includes an association of producers, sellers,
distributors, traders or service providers who, by agreement
amongst themselves, limit, control or attempt to control the
production, distribution, sale or price of, or, trade in goods or
provision of services.
(4) Any agreement amongst enterprises or persons at different
stages or levels of the production chain in different markets, in respect
of production, supply, distribution, storage, sale or price of, or trade
in goods or provision of services, including—
(a) tie-in arrangement;
(b) exclusive supply agreement;
(c) exclusive distribution agreement;
(d) refusal to deal;
(e) resale price maintenance;
shall be an agreement in contravention of sub-section (1) if such
agreement causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on
competition.
Explanation—For the purposes of this sub-section,—
(a) “tie-in arrangements” includes any agreement requiring
a purchaser of goods, as a condition of such purchase, to
purchase some other goods;
(b) “exclusive supply agreement” includes any agreement
restricting in any manner the purchaser in the course of his
trade from acquiring or otherwise dealing in any goods other
than those of the seller or any other person;
(c) “exclusive distribution agreement” includes any
agreement to limit, restrict or withhold the output or supply of
any goods or allocate any area or market for the disposal or
sale of the goods;

93
(d) “refusal to deal” includes any agreement which restricts,
or is likely to restrict, by any method the persons or classes of
persons to whom goods are sold or from whom goods are
bought;
(e) “resale price maintenance” includes any agreement to
sell goods on condition that the prices to be charged on the
resale by the purchaser shall be the prices stipulated by the
seller unless it is clearly stated that prices lower than those
prices may be charged;
(5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to-
(a) “copyright” under the Copyright Act, 1957;
(b) “patent” or “exclusive right” granted under the Patents
Act, 1970;
(c) “collective mark”, “permitted use”, “registered
proprietor”, “registered trade mark” or “registered user” under
the Trade Marks Act, 1999;
(d) “homonymous geographical indication” or “geographical
indications” registered under the Geographical Indications of
Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999;
(e) “design” registered under the Designs Act, 2000;
(f) “layout-design” registered under the Semi-conductor
Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000;
(g) the right of any person to export goods from India
to the extent to which the agreement relates exclusively to the
production, supply, distribution or control of goods or provision
of services for such export.

7. (1) With effect from such date as the Central Government
may, by notification appoint, there shall be established, for the
purposes of this Act, a Commission to be called the “Competition
Commission of lndia”.
(2) The Commission shall be a body corporate by the name
aforesaid having perpetual succession and a common seal with power,
subject to the provisions of this Act, to acquire, hold and dispose of
property, both movable and immovable, and to contract and shall, by
the said name, sue or be sued.
(3) The head office of the Commission shall be at such
place as the Central Government may decide from time to time.
(4) The Commission may establish offices at other places
in India.
8. (1) The Commission shall consist of a Chairperson and
not less than two and not more than ten other Members to be
appointed by the Central Government:
Provided that the Central Government shall appoint the
Chairperson and a Member during the first year of the establishment
of the Commission.
(2) The Chairperson and every other Member shal1 be the
persons of ability, integrity and standing, who—
(a) are, or have been, or are qualified to be, a Judge of
a High Court; or
(b) have special knowledge of, and professional experience
in, not less than fifteen years, international trade, economics,
business, commerce, law, finance, accountancy, management,
industry, public affairs, administration or in any other matter
which, in the opinion of the Central Government, be useful to
the Commission.
(3) The Chairperson and other Members shall be whole-time
Members.
9. ( 1) The Chairperson and every other Member shall be
appointed by the Central Government on the recommendation of a
Selection Committee consisting of—
(a) the Chief Justice of India or his nominee – Chairperson;
(b) the Union Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of
Finance – Member;

advantages over competitors;

In the pursuit of globalisation, India has responded by opening up its
economy, removing controls and resorting to liberalisation. The natural corollary
of this is that the Indian market should be geared to face competition from
within the country and outside. The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
Act, 1969 has become obsolete in certain respects in the light of international
economic developments relating more particularly to competition laws and there
is a need to shift our focus from curbing monopolies to promoting competition.
2. The Central Government constituted a High Level Committee on
Competition Policy and Law. The Committee submitted its report on the
22nd May, 2000 to the Central Government. The Central Government consulted
all concerned including the trade and industry associations and the general
public. The Central Government after considering the suggestions of the trade
and industry and the general public decided to enact a law on Competition.
3. The Competition Bill, 2001 seeks to ensure fair competition in India by
prohibiting trade practices which cause appreciable adverse effect on competition
in markets within India and, for this purpose, provides for the establishment of
a quasi-judicial body to be called the Competition Commission of India
(hereinafter referred to as CCI) which shall also undertake competition advocacy
for creating awareness and imparting training on competition issues.
4. The Bill also aims at curbing negative aspects of competition through the
medium of CCI. CCI will have a Principal Bench and Additional Benches and will
also have one or more Mergers Benches. It will look into violations of the Act,
a task which could be undertaken by the Commission based on its own
knowledge or information or complaints received and reference made by the
Central Government, the State Governments or statutory authorities. The
Commission can pass orders for granting interim relief or any other appropriate
relief and compensation or an order imposing penalties etc. An appeal from the
orders of the Commission shall lie to the Supreme Court. The Central.
Government will also have powers to issue directions to the Commission on
policy matters after considering its suggestions as well as the power to
supersede the Commission if such a situation is warranted.
5. The Bill also provides for investigation by the Director-General for the
Commission. The Director-General would be able to act only if so directed by
the Commission but will not have any suo-moto powers for initiating
investigations.
6. The Bill confers power upon the CCI to levy penalty for contravention
of its orders, failure to comply with its directions, making of false statements
or omission to furnish material information, etc. The CCI can levy upon an
enterprise a penalty of not more than ten percent of its average turn-over for
the last three financial years. It can also order division of dominant enterprises.
It will also have power to order demerger in the case of mergers and
amalgamations that adversely, affect competition.
129

130
7. The Bill also seeks to create a fund to be called the Competition Fund.
The grants given by the Central Government, costs realised by the Commission
and application fees charged will be credited into this Fund. The pay and
allowances and the other expenses of the Commission will also be borne out of
this Fund. The Bill provides for empowering the Comptroller and Auditor-General
of India to audit the accounts of the Commission. The Central Government will
be required to lay the annual accounts of the Commission, as audited by the
Comptroller and Auditor-General and also the annual report of the Commission
before both the Houses of Parliament.
8. The Bill aims at repealing the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
Act, 1969 and the dissolution of the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
Commission. The Bill provides that the cases pending before the Monopolies and
Restrictive Trade Practices Commission will be transferred to the CCI except
those relating to unfair trade practices which are proposed to be transferred to
the relevant for a established under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
9. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

PRESIDENT’S RECOMMENDATIONS UNDER ARTICLE 117 OF THE
CONSTITUTION OF INDIA
[Copy of letter No. PC-5/23/2000-IGC, dated the 30th July, 2001 from
Shri Arun Jaitley, Minister of law, Justice and Company Affairs to the Secretary-
General, Lok Sabha]
The President, having been informed of the subject matter of the proposed
Competition Bill, 2001 has recommended its introduction in Lok Sabha under
article 117(1) of the Constitution and for its consideration by Lok Sabha under
article 117(3) of the Constitution.

Notes on Clauses
Clause 1.— This clause, inter alia, seeks to extend the provisions of the
Bill to the whole of India excluding the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
Clause 2.— This clause defines various expressions used in the Bill.
Clause 3.— This Clause, inter alia, provides for prohibition of entering
into anticompetitive agreements. It shall not be lawful for  any enterprise or
association of enterprises, or person or association of persons to enter into an
agreement in respect of production, supply, storage, distribution, acquisition or
control of goods or provision of service which causes or is likely to cause an
appreciable adverse effect on competition within India. All such agreements
entered into in contravention of the aforesaid prohibition shall be void. This
clause also specifies certain activities which shall be presumed to have an
appreciable adverse effect on competition and also specifies certain agreements
which shall be in adverse effect on competition and also specifies certain
agreements which shall be in contravention of sub-clause (1) of the said clause
if such agreement causes appreciable adverse on competition. The provision of
this clause shall not apply to certain rights specified in sub-clause (5) of this
clause.
Clause 4.— This clause prohibits abuse of dominant position by any
enterprise. Such abuse of dominant position, inter alia, includes imposition,
either directly or indirectly, of unfair or discriminatory purchase or selling prices
or conditions, including predatory prices of goods or service, limiting production
or restricting of goods or provision of service, indulging in practices resulting
in denial of market access, making the conclusion of contracts subject to
acceptance by other parties of supplementary obligations and using dominant
position in one market to enter into or protect other market.
Clause 5.— This clause deals with combination of enterprises and
persons. The acquisition of one or more enterprises by one or more persons or
acquiring of control or merger or amalgamation of enterprises under certain
circumstances specified in the said clause shall be construed as combination.
Clause. 6.— This clause, inter alia, provides that no person or enterprise
shall enter into a combination which is likely to cause or causes an appreciable
adverse effect on competition within the relevant market in India. It further
provides exemption from the provisions of this clause to certain institutions
specified in sub-clause (2) of the said clause.
Clause 7.— This clause provides for the establishment of the
Competition Commission of India. The commission shall be a body corporate by
the aforesaid name having perpetual succession and a common seal with power
to acquire, hold and dispose of property. The place of head office of the
Commission shall be decided by the Central Government. However, the
Commission can establish offices at other places in India.

132

The Commission shall consist of the Chairperson and not less than two and not
more than ten other members, as may be specified by the Central Government.
However the Central Government shall appoint the Chairperson and a member
during first year of the establishment of the Commission. This clause also lays
down that the Chairperson and other Members shall be persons of  ability,
integrity and standing. A person who is or has been or  is qualified to be a Judge
of a High Court or is having special knowledge of,  and professional experience
in, not less than fifteen years in international trade, economics, business,
commerce, law, finance, accountancy, management, industry, public affairs,
administration or in any other matter which, in the opinion of the central
Government, be useful to the Commission, shall be eligible for appointment as
the Chairperson or as a Member.

Chairperson and Members of the Commission. The appointment shall be made by
the Central Government on the recommendation of the Selection Committee
consisting of the Chief Justice of India or his nominee, the Union Minister-in-
charge of the Ministry of finance, the Union Minister-in-charge of the Ministry
of Department of the Central government dealing with the proposed legislation,
the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India and the cabinet Secretary. However,
an appointment made to the office of the Chairperson or a Member shall not be
invalid merely on the ground that there is any defect in the constitution of the
Selection Committee or any vacancy therein.

five years. This clause also provides for discharge of functions of the
Chairperson by the senior-most member in case the Chairperson is unable to
discharge his functions.

resignation, removal and suspension of the chairperson and other Members. Sub-

the Chairperson or a Member in respect of whom a reference has been made
to the Supreme Court. Sub-clause (4) provides for other circumstances under
which the Chairperson or any Member can be removed from office by the
Central Government.
Clause 12.— This clause provides that the Chairperson or a Member

the Commission. However, such a restriction of employment shall not apply in
case of any employment under the Central Government or a State Government

133
or a local authority or a statutory authority or corporation established by a

superintendence, direction and control in respect of all administrative maters of

terms and conditions of service of the Chairperson and other members of the

service of the Chairperson and other members shall not be varied to their
disadvantage after their appointment.

or under the proposed legislation. It also empowers the Central Government to
specify, by rules, their qualifications, the salary and allowances payable to them

Clause 17.— This clause empowers the Commission to appoint Registrar

market constitutes a relevant market for the purposes of the proposed legislation.

Benches of the Commission and exercise of the jurisdiction, powers and

Clause 26.— This clause lays down the detailed procedure for any
inquiry initiated suo motu by the Commission and various complaints and

Clause 60.— This clause seeks to provide that the provisions of the
proposed legislation shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, the
provisions of any other law for the time being in force.
Clause 61.— This clause confers upon the Central Government the
power to make rules to carry out the provisions of the proposed legislation. Sub-
clause (2) of this clause enumerates the various matters in respect of which
such rules may be made. Sub-clause (3) provides that every notification issued
under sub-clause (3) of clause 20 and Clause 52 and every rule made by the

Clause 62.— This clause confers power upon the Commission to make
regulations consistent with the proposed legislation and the rules made

thereunder, to carry out the purposes of the proposed legislations. Sub-clause (2)
enumerates the various matters in respect of which such regulations may be
made by the Commission. Sub-clause (3) provides for laying of regulations
before both Houses of Parliament.
Clause 63.— This clause seeks to empower the Central Government to
made provision, by order, published in the official Gazatte, to remove difficulties
which may arise in giving effect to the provisions of the Bill. However, such
order can be issued only within a period of two years from the date of
commencement of the proposed legislation. The orders made under this clause
shall be required to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
Clause 64.— This clause provides for repeal and savings. This clause,
inter alia, proposes to repeal the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
Act, 1969. Upon such repeal, the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices
Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 5 of the said Act shall
stand dissolved. Sub-clauses (2) to (10) deal with the matters arising out of
such repeal.

Sub-clause (1) of clause 7 of the Bill provides for the establishment of
a Commission to be known as the Competition Commission of India with effect
from such date as the Central Government may, by notification, appoint in this
behalf. Sub-clause (3) provides that the head office of the Commission shall be
at such place as the Central Government may decide. Sub-clause (4) enables the
Commission to establish offices at other places in India.
2. Sub-clause (1) of clause 8 of the Bill provides that the Commission
shall consist of a Chairperson and not less than two and not more than ten other
Members to be appointed by the Central Government. During first year of its
establishment, the Commission shall consist of a Chairperson and one Member.
The Chairperson and other Members shall be the whole-time Members.
3. Sub-clause (1) of clause 14 of the Bill provides that the Chairperson
shall be entitled to a salary equal to the salary of a Judge of the Supreme Court.
Sub-clause (2) provides that a Member shall be paid salary equal to that of a
Judge of a High Court. Sub-clause (3) provides that the other conditions of
service relating to travelling expenses, provision of house rent allowance and
conveyance facilities, sumptuary allowance and medical facilities shall be such as
may be specified by rules made by the Central Government.
4. Clause 16 of the Bill provides for appointment of a Director General
and as many Additional, Joint, Deputy or Assistant Directors General as the
Central Government may think fit for assisting the Commission in conducting
inquiry into contravention of the provisions of the proposed legislation and for
performing such other functions as may be provided by or under the proposed
legislation. Sub-clause (3) provides that the salary, allowances and other
conditions of service of the Director General, Additional, Joint, Deputy or
Assistant Directors General shall be such as may be prescribed by the Central
Government.

appoint a Registrar and such officers and employees of the Commission as it

payable and other terms and conditions of service of the Registrar, other officers
and employees of the Commission shall be such as may be prescribed by the
Central Government.

authority of the Commission may be exercised by Benches thereof. The

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorized
by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninty-fourth Report on the Supreme Court Judges
(Salaries and Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 2002·.
 
2.         In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya
Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ¨¨ theSupreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service)
Amendment Bill, 2002, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 17 May 2002 and pending therein, to the Committee on 28 May 2002
for examination and report.
 
3.0.      The Committee considered the Bill in three sittings held on 3 July, 22 August and  9 September 2002.
 
3.1       The Committee heard oral evidence of the  Additional Secretary, Department of Justice (Ministry of Law and Justice) on
the Bill in its sitting held on 3 July 2002. In the same sitting and also in its sitting held on 22 August 2002, the Committee held
deliberations on the Bill.
 
3.2       In its sitting held on 9 September 2002, the Committee considered the draft Report on the Bill and adopted the same. In
the same sitting the Committee also decided that the evidence tendered before the Committee may be laid on the Table of both
the Houses of Parliament.
 
4.         In the course of preparation of its Report, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received form
the Department of Justice (Ministry of Law and Justice) and replies of the Department of Justice to the queries raised by the
Chairman and Members of the Committee.
 
5.         For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in
bold letters in the body of the Report.
 
NEWDELHI
9 September 2002
PRANABMUKHERJEE
Chairman
Committee on Home Affairs
 
 
REPORT
 
            The Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Amendment Bill, 2002 (See Annexure-I) seeks to
provide for addition of five years of service to the pensionable service in the case of those Judges of the Supreme Court who are
elevated directly from the Bar, to enable them to get the full pension, to the extent of the maximum ceiling of Rs.1,80,000 per
year.
 
2.0       The Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 (41 of 1958) and the rules made thereunder
govern and regulate the salaries and other conditions of service including pension of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
 
2.1       Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are placed in three categories for the purpose of computation of basic
pension1
:-
           
(i)            Part I       :   These Judges are elevated directly from the Bar.
           
(ii)            Part II     : These Judges are elevated from the Indian Civil Service 2.                                                        
           
(iii)            Part III   :   These Judges are elevated from the State Judicial Services.
 
3.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill states -
“An advocate having practice of at least ten years in a High Court or in two or more such Courts in succession can
directly be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court under the provisions of sub-clause (b) of clause (3) of article 124
of the Constitution.  As per the convention, no such advocate below the age of 55 years is normally considered for
appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court.  The pension to a Part I Judge (who is elevated from the Bar) is payable in
accordance with the provisions of section 13 read with Part I of the Schedule to the Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and
Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 and accordingly, the maximum pension of Rs.1,80,000 per annum is payable to a Judge

94th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/94threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:55:46]
of the Supreme Court after he renders a minimum service of 13 years (at the rate of Rs.14,630 for each completed year
of service on his retirement).  It is felt that Part I Judges can never have enough completed years of service entitling them
to earn full pension.  In the case of Judges not completing 7 years of minimum service, a fixed amount of Rs.64,030 per
annum is payable as pension.
 
A former Chief Justice of India, while forwarding a representation from one such Judge, suggested that provision be
made for grant of pension to such Judges by adding, about 7 to 10 years period to the tenure of service rendered in the
Supreme Court.
 
To remove anomaly between Part I and Part III Judges of the Supreme Court as regards their entitlement to pension and
to give incentive to the eminent advocates who are meritorious and talented to come forward to be appointed as Supreme
Court Judges, it is proposed to amend the said Act to provide five years added benefit of service to a Judge of the
Supreme Court for the purpose of his pension”.
 
4.         The Committee heard the Additional Secretary, Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice in its meeting held
on 3 July 2002 wherein he inter-alia stated that in September 2000, the then Chief Justice of India forwarded an application from
Mr. Justice Kuldip Singh dated 8 August 2000 complaining of inequity in the matter of similarly placed Judges of the Supreme
Court in regard to pension (SeeAnnexure II).  He further stated that the matter was considered by the then Law Minister and
examined in consultation with related Ministries and found that there were parallel provisions in the Central Civil Service
(Pensions) Rules, 1972.  He cited Rule 30 of CCS (Pensions) Rules, which authorizes the Government to add a period, not
exceeding five years, to the pensionable service of an officer in the government whose service conditions require special
qualifications or professional experience.  It was noticed that members of the Bar, who are appointed under Article 124 (3)(b) of
the Constitution also come with specialized qualifications and professional experience and thus can be given benefit of adding
five years service for the purpose of pension.
 
5.0       The witness further stated, that in the States such as Punjab there is a provision which authorizes the Government to add
a period, not exceeding ten years, to the pensionable service of a Judicial Officer in view of his practice at the Bar.  This
provision coupled with Rule 30 of the Central Civil Service (Pension) Rules, 1972 led the Government to introduce the Bill.
 
5.1       He also informed that the proposed legislation will benefit three retired Judges, namely, Mr. Justice S.C. Roy, Mr.
Justice S.M. Sikri and Mr. Justice Kuldip Singh, a sitting Judge, Mr. Justice Hegde and all other such future appointees who
would be   appointed from the Bar. 
 
6.         It may be mentioned here that besides writing to the Law Minister, Mr. Justice Kuldip Singh petitioned the Supreme
Court in this regard which is still pending at the time of writing this report.
 
7.0       The Committee wanted to know as to what was the rationale behind the practice being followed that advocates of less
than 55 years of age are not appointed directly from the Bar to the Bench of the Supreme Court when the Constitution under
Article 124 provides for appointment of advocates with at least 10 years of practice at the Bar to the Supreme Court.
 
7.1       The Ministry, in its written reply, justified that keeping in view the guidelines prescribing the age limit of 40-45 years for
appointment as a Judge of the High Court and qualifications prescribed for a Judge of Supreme Court in Article 124 (3) (a)  & 
(b) of the Constitution, this convention helped in maintaining a sort of age parity between the Judges of the Supreme Court
appointed from the Bench and the Bar. 
 
8.0       The Committee observes that the judiciary itself has initiated the practice of appointing only those advocates who are not
less than 55 years of age to be a Judge of the Supreme Court whereas the Constitution has prescribed 10 years’ practice at the
Bar.  It, therefore, fails to comprehend as to why the Government now requires a legislation to wriggle out of the situation which
has been created due to the said practice.
 
8.1       After having heard the presentation of the Additional Secretary, Department of Justice on 3 July 2002, having gone
through the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill and background notes received from the same Department and also
holding  detailed discussion, the Committee has come to the conclusion that there is no principle involved in the proposed
legislative measure as it is meant to benefit a few Judges only. Besides, the Committee feels that when the petition is already
before the Supreme Court, legislative recourse should not be taken to legitimize the measure.  The Committee, therefore, feels
that the Government may explore other possibilities to achieve the objective of the Bill.
 
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS  AT A GLANCE

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            The Supreme Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Act, 1958 (41 of 1958) was enacted to regulate the
salaries and certain conditions of service of the Judges of the Supreme Court.  An advocate having practice of at least ten years
in a High Court or in two or more such Courts in succession can directly be appointed as a Judge of the Supreme Court under
the provisions of sub-clause (b) of clause (3) of article 124 of the Constitution. As per the convention, no such advocate below
the age of 55 years is normally considered for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court.  The pension to a Part I Judge (who
is elevated from the Bar) is payable in accordance with the provisions of section 13 read with Part I of the Schedule to the said
Act, and accordingly, the maximum pension of Rs. 1,80,000 per annum is payable to a Judge of the Supreme Court after he

that Part I Judges can never have enough completed years of service entitling them to earn full pension.  In the case of Judges
not completing 7 years of minimum service, a fixed amount of Rs. 64,030 per annum is payable as pension.
 
            2. A former Chief Justice of India, while forwarding a representation from one such Judge, suggested that provision be
made for grant of pension to such Judges by adding about 7 to 10 years period to the tenure of service rendered in the Supreme
Court.
 
            3. To remove anomaly between Part I and Part III Judges of the Supreme Court as regards their entitlement to pension
and to give incentive to the eminent advocates who are meritorious and talented to come forward to be appointed as Supreme
Court Judges, it is proposed to amend the said Act to provide five years added benefit of service to a Judge of the Supreme
Court for the purpose of his pension.

2.         My appointment was in terms of Article 124 (3) (b) above.  I retired from the office on January 1, 1997.  My pension has
been fixed in terms of the Presidential Order dated January 13, 1999 issued by the Ministry of Law, Government of India. 
Under the said Order a Judge of the Supreme Court retiring with seven or more completed years of service, his pension is fixed
by applying the multiplier “Rs.14,630 X Number of years served” subject to the maximum of “Rs.1,80,000”.  I served as a
Judge for 8 years and 18 days.  My pension per annum has been fixed by multiplying Rs. 14,630/-by 8.
 
3.         The pension-fixation formula is on the face of it causing hardship to the appointees under Article 124 (3) (b).  It is
almost an established convention that no Advocate below the age of 55 years is considered for appointment to the Supreme
Court.  As such the Judges appointed under the Article 124 (3) (b)  can never have enough completed years  of service to claim
full pension.  On the other hand the appointees to the Supreme Court from the High Courts have invariably more than 10 years
of service as Judges of the High Courts to their credit and while fixing pension, their entire service as a High Court Judges is
also taken into consideration.  Almost all of them enjoy the maximum pension. 
 
4.         There are more than twenty brother Judges (retired) who were junior to me in the Supreme Court and have served as
Supreme Court Judge for lesser years than me but all of them are drawing more pension than me.  A rule which permits a higher
pension to a person who has served 3 years as a Supreme Court judge and a lesser pension to another who has served 8 years as
a Supreme Court judge is on the face of it arbitrary.
 
5.         I am the only retired Supreme Court Judge as at present, who was appointed direct from the Bar.  One way of doing
justice to the direct appointees to the Supreme Court is to add the eligibility period of 10 years as an advocate to the actual years
spent in the Supreme Court and pension fixed on that basis.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Ninety-fifth Report of the
Committee on the Repatriation of Prisoners Bill, 2002.
2.         In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred ** the Repatriation of Prisoners Bill, 2002 as
introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 9 May 2002 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Bill in its sittings held on 3 July, 9 September and 9 October 2002.
 
3.1       The Committee took oral evidence of the Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs in its sitting held on 3
July 2002.
 
3.2       In its sitting held on 9 September 2002, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
 
3.3       The Committee considered the draft Report on the Bill and adopted the same in its sitting held on 9 October
2002.
 
4.         In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background note on the Bill received from
the Ministry of Home Affairs and replies of the Ministry to the queries raised by the Members in its sittings.
 
5.
                  For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been
printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
           
NEW DELHI;
October 9, 2002.
PRANAB MUKHERJEE
                                                                                                                                Chairman
                           Committee on Home Affairs
 
*   Bill published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II, Section-2, dated 9 May, 2002.
** Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, No. 39802 dated 28 May 2002.
            
REPORT
            The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Repatriation of Prisoners Bill, 2002 (Annexure-I) states
that in the absence of any legal provision either in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 or any other law under which a
foreign prisoner could be transferred outside the country, there has been long detention of foreign prisoners in the jails
causing thereby considerable concern to the Government of India as well as the concerned foreign Governments.  It
was, therefore, felt that if foreign convicted nationals were transferred to their home countries to serve their remaining
jail terms, it would take care of the human aspect inasmuch as the convicts would be near their families and have better
chances of social rehabilitation.  In addition, it would also take care of the problems which the Indian jail authorities are
facing in keeping these prisoners. Thus, the Bill proposes legislation, in conjunction with bilateral treaties to enable the
Central Government to transfer foreign convicted persons to their country and vice versa.
 
2.         The salient features of the proposed legislation inter alia are as follows:
(a)
                a request for transfer will have to be made by the convicted prisoner or a person entitled to act on his
behalf in view of his age or physical or mental condition;
(b)               the request for transfer will have to be agreed upon by the transferring State and the receiving State;
(c)                the transfer will be effected if the judgement awarding the sentence is final in India i.e. no appeal or

95th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/95threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:55:46]
revision against the judgement is pending in any court;
(d)               the transfer will be made if the convicted prisoner is a citizen of the receiving State notwithstanding that
he may also be citizen of any other foreign state;
(e)                the enforcement of the sentence shall be governed by the law of the receiving State.  However, the
receiving State shall be bound by the legal nature and duration of the sentence as determined by the
transferring State;
(f)                 the enforcement of the sentence in the receiving State, to the extent that it has been enforced in the
transferring State, shall have the effect of discharing the sentence;
(g)                the transferring State alone shall be competent to decide any application for review of the judgement
and grant pardon, amnesty or commutation in accordance with its constitution or other laws;
(h)                The convicted person shall not be transferred if-
 
(i)         the transferring State is of the opinion that the request would prejudice its sovereignty, security,
national interest or other essential interests;
(ii)                any other case is pending in the transferring State against the convicted prisoner;
(iii)               he is convicted of an offence under military law not being an offence under the ordinary
criminal law of the transferring State; and
(iv)              the death penalty has been awarded to the convicted prisoner in the transferring State.
 
3.         In its background note on the Bill, the Ministry of Home Affairs has informed the Committee that there is
presently no legal provision under which foreign prisoners can be transferred to the country of their origin to serve their
sentence there nor is there any provision for the transfer of the persons of Indian origin convicted by a foreign court, to
serve their sentence here.  In the absence of legislative provision, it is not possible to execute treaties/agreements with
foreign Governments for transfer of convicted prisoners.  This apart, the sentences awarded by foreign courts cannot be
acted upon under the existing laws.
 
3.1       It has been further stated that the complaints have been received from time to time regarding long detention of
foreign prisoners in jails pending investigation and trial, and alleged unsatisfactory living conditions in which they are
kept.  Though the total number of foreign nationals in jails has never been very large yet they have been causing
considerable concern to the Government.  At the end of the year 1999, there were 665 foreign convicted and 1486
undertrial prisoners in different jails of the country.
 
3.2       The background note further states that those and other related issues concerning foreigners in jails were
discussed at a very high level meeting where it was inter alia decided to amend the Code of Criminal Procedure and/or
the transfer of Prisoners Act, 1950 for making an enabling provision for transfer of convicted prisoners from one
country to another.  The Ministry of Law and Justice was, however, of the view that a new legislation  may be enacted
for the transfer of foreign prisoners to the country of their origin on the lines of the Commonwealth Scheme for the
transfer of convicted offenders.
 
3.3       The background note goes on to state that in the recent past, the Government has negotiated agreements with the
Governments of United Kingdom, France and Norway in regard to the transfer of convicted offenders.  Similar
agreements with the Governments of other countries are under discussion.  However, in the absence of an enabling
legislation, these agreements cannot be acted upon.
 
3.4       The background note adds that accordingly a note dated 30 October 1996  was  submitted seeking approval of
the Cabinet for enacting legislation to enable the transfer of convicted foreign prisoners to the countries of their origin
and vice versa.  In its meeting held on 12 November 1996, the Cabinet considered the said proposal and approved the
same.  However, before the Bill in this regard could be proposed and introduced in Parliament, the Eleventh Lok Sabha
was dissolved on 4 December 1997.  In order to proceed further in the matter, a note dated 1 July 1998 was placed
before the Cabinet.  In its meeting held on 7 July 1998, the Cabinet considered the note, but did not approve the
proposal.  Considering the necessity of the proposed legislation, the Cabinet note was again submitted and was approved

95th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/95threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:55:46]
in the Cabinet meeting held on 23 September 2001. 
 
3.5       The background note concludes that the proposed legislation in conjunction with bilateral treaties would enable
the Government to transfer the foreign convicted offenders to the country of their origin and receive Indian citizens
serving sentences in a country or place outside India.  Its provisions shall apply to the enforcement of sentences imposed
before as well as after the enactment of the law.
 
4.         The Bill consists of 16 clauses which were considered and adopted by the Committee as mentioned in the
succeeding paragraphs.
 
Clause 2
 
4.1       The clause contains the definitions of various terminology required to be used in the enactment.
 
4.2       A point was raised by the Committee regarding the definition of ‘prisoner’ as prescribed in clause 2(c)  as to
whether the prisoners sent to the jail by the Civil Court were also included in the definition.  The written response of the
Ministry of Home Affairs in this regard is reproduced below:
 
“The definition of prisoner under clause 2 (c ) provides that prisoner means a person undergoing a sentence of
imprisonment under an order passed by Criminal Court including a Court established under the law for the time
being in force in contracting State.  The definition of the word “prisoner” does not include a prisoner sent to jail
by a Civil Court.  There is, therefore, no ambiguity in the definition of prisoner who are covered under the
proposed law”.
 
4.3       Regarding the word “warrant”, the Committee wanted to know whether the ‘warrant’ as stipulated in the clause,
can be issued by a  Joint Secretary to the Government.
 
4.4       The  Ministry of Home Affairs  furnished the comments of the Ministry of Law and Justice as  given below:
 
“It may be noted that warrant contemplated under section 105 and 105B, Cr.P.C. is a warrant for arrest of a
person, who is free, but the warrant conceived under clauses 7(1) and 8 of the Bill is not a warrant for arrest, but
a warrant only to deliver the custody of a prisoner to the person authorized by the contracting State to which the
prisoner is to be transferred.  There seems to be no conflict between the provisions of the Cr.P.C. and the Bill, as
the nature of the warrants under the two are different”.
 
4.5       The clause is adopted without any change.
 
Clause 3
 
4.6       The clause deals with the application of the Act.
 
4.7       Regarding sub-clause (3) of the clause,  the Committee wanted to know as to whether the sub-clause proposed to
give power to the Central Government to circumvent and modify legal/judicial processes on the strength of a simple
notification in the Official Gazette.  The clarification  of Ministry of Home Affairs is reproduced below:
 
“Clause 3(3) of the Bill provides that if  the Central Government is of the opinion that with respect to a country
or place outside India, provisions of this Act require to be modified to give effect to a treaty in relation to such
country, it may, by notification in the Official Gazette, direct that the application of this Act to such country
shall be subject to such conditions, exceptions and modifications specified in the notification.  This clause does
not empower the Central Government to alter the mandatory legislative intentions.  This provision only
authorizes the Central Government to make required modifications to give effect to a treaty with another country
subject to certain conditions and exceptions to be specified in the Official notification.  Such notification may be
complementary and not in conflict with the substantive provisions.  In this connection kind attention is also
invited to Section 105L, Cr.P.C. as well as Section 3 (3) (c ) of the Extradition Act, 1962, which are similar to

State”.

replied that as mentioned in clause 3, the legislation aimed at the transfer of prisoner between the contracting States.

4.19     The clause is adopted without any change.

4.21     The clause is adopted without any change.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
           
Long detention of foreign prisoners in Indian jails has been causing considerable concern to the Government of
India and the foreign Governments concerned. It was, therefore, felt that if foreign convicted nationals were transferred
to their home countries to serve their remaining jail terms, it would take care of the human aspect inasmuch as the said
convicts would be near their families and have better chances of social rehabilitation.  Further, it would also take care of
the problems which the Indian jail authorities are facing in keeping these prisoners.  There is presently no legal
provision either in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 or any other law under which a foreign prisoner could be
transferred outside India.  The Bill proposes legislation, in conjunction with bilateral treaties to enable the Central
Government to transfer foreign convicted persons to their country and vice versa.
2.         The salient features of the proposed legislation inter alia, are as follows:-
            (a)        a request for transfer will have to be made by the convicted prisoner or a person entitled to act on his
behalf in view of his age or physical or mental condition;
            (b)        the request for transfer will have to be agreed upon by the transferring State and the receiving State;
            (c )       the transfer will be effected if the judgement awarding the sentence is final in India i.e. no appeal or
revision against the judgement is pending in any court;
            (d)        the transfer will be made if the convicted prisoner is a citizen of the receiving State notwithstanding that
he may also be citizen of any other foreign State;
            (e)        the enforcement of the sentence shall be governed by the law of the receiving State.  However, the
receiving State shall be bound by the legal nature and duration of the sentence as determined by the transferring State;
            (f)        the enforcement of the sentence in the receiving State, to the extent that it has been enforced in the
transferring State, shall have the effect of discharging the sentence;
            (g)        the transferring State alone shall be competent to decide any application for review of the judgement and
grant pardon, amnesty or commutation in accordance with its constitution or other laws;
(h)        the convicted person shall not be transferred if-
(i)         the transferring State is of the opinion that the request would prejudice its sovereignty, security,
national interest or other essential interests;
(ii)        any other case is pending in the transferring State against the convicted prioner;
(iii)
             he is convicted of an offence under military law not being an offence under the ordinary criminal
law of the transferring State; and
(iv)       the death penalty has been awarded to the convicted prisoner in the transferring State.
 
3.         The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

            The proposed legislation aims at providing for the transfer of certain prisoners from  India to a country or place
outside India and reception in India of certain prisoners from a country or place outside India.  This legislation would be
implemented in conjunction with bilaterial treaties as provided in clause 3 of the Bill.

AN OVERVIEW OF THE SWATANTRATA SAINIK SAMMAN PENSION SCHEME, 
1980  
 
2. In 1969, a Scheme, known as “Ex-Andaman Political Prisoners Pension Scheme” was 
launched.  Under the Scheme, pension was sanctioned to those freedom fighters who had suffered 
imprisonment in the Cellular Jail, Port Blair (Andaman Islands) for a minimum period of five 
years.  In 1972, on the occasion of 25
th Anniversary (Silver Jublilee) of Independence, a regular 
Freedom Fighters’ Pension Scheme was introduced covering other categories of freedom fighters.  
In 1980, the scheme was liberalized and renamed as “Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension 
Scheme”.  Liberalisation was done in the following areas: 
 
(a) The income limit of Rs.5000/- per annum under the 1972 scheme was removed 
and pension was viewed as a token of ‘Samman’. 
(b) Minimum period of imprisonment was reduced from six months to three months 
for women and SC/ST freedom fighters. 
(c) Under the 1972 scheme, evidence from official record was required to prove 
underground/externment/internment sufferings.  Under the new scheme, if the 
records were not available, corrobora tive evidence by way of certificates from 
prominent freedom fighters, with proven ja il sufferings of two years or more and 
belonging to the district of the applicant, was accepted. 
 
A list of recognized movements/mutinies for Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension (SSSP) 
is at Annexure-I. 
 
ELIGIBILITY CONDITIONS 
 
3. Every person who took part in the freedom struggle is not eligible for pension under the 
scheme.  Only those freedom fighters, who ha d undergone the prescribed minimum sufferings, 
are eligible.  The minimum sufferings which make a freedom fighter eligible for pension are: 
 
(a) A person who had suffered a minimum im prisonment of six months in the 
mainland jails before Independence.  Ex-INA personnel are also eligible for 
pension if the imprisonment/detention suffe red by them was outside India for six 
months or more.  In case of women and SC/ST freedom fighters, the minimum 
period of actual imprisonment for eligibility of pension is three months. 
(b) A person who remained underground for six months or more provided he was:- 
(i) a proclaimed offender; 
(ii) one on whom an award for arrest/head was announced; or 
(iii) one whose detention order was issued but not served. 
 7

(c ) A person who was interned in his home or externed from his district under the 
orders of the competent authority for six months or more. 
(d) A person whose property was confiscat ed or attached and sold due to 
participation in the National Freedom Struggle. 
(e) A person who was permanently incapac itated during firing or lathi charge. 
(f) A person who lost his Government job (including job in a local body) for 
participation in the National Freedom Struggle. 
(g) A person who was awarded the punishment of 10 strokes of 
caning/flogging/whipping. 
 
4. To become eligible for pension an app licant has to submit documentary evidence duly 
verified by the State Government along w ith their recommendation as required under the SSSP 
Scheme.

(b) Free air travel facility to visit Port Blair once a year from Chennai/Calcutta along

(c) Facility to travel in Shatabadi/Rajdhani Express trains along with companion. 
 
6. Under the Freedom Fighters Pension Scheme, 1972 and the Swatantrata Sainik Samman 
Pension Scheme, 1980, the last dates prescribed fo r receipt of applications were 31.3.1974 and 
31.3.1982, respectively. 
 
6.1 However, applications kept pouring in ther eafter too.  The position with regard to receipt 
of applications under the old scheme of 1972, under the liberalized Scheme of 1980 (upto 
31.3.1982) and thereafter is given hereunder.

7. As many as 2,39,290 applications have been received after the cut-off date for grant of 
Samman Pension.  The primary reason for such a deluge of applications was relaxation made in 
the 1980 Scheme with regard to production of secondary evidence i.e. Co-prisoner Certificate 
 9

(CPC) and Personal Knowledge Certificate (P KC) in the absence of primary documentary 
evidence from the official records.   
 
7.1 In view of the large number of applicati ons received after the cut-off date, and following 
the recommendations of the Committee on Petitions , Rajya Sabha, as contained in its Ninety-
seventh Report presented to Rajya Sabha on 9 August 1989, a proposal was submitted for 
consideration of the Cabinet, for the closure of the Scheme vide Note dated February 27, 1992.  
In the Note, approval of the Cabinet was solicited to the proposals – (a) the existing system of 
considering and deciding the cases, with referenc e to the terms and conditions of the Schemes 
already approved, may continue; (b) cases already rejected, at the level of Joint Secretary and 
above, should not ordinarily be re-opened for fresh consideration; (c) where however, new strong 
evidence was adduced and it prima facie justifies re-opening of the case, an exception may be 
made and the case reconsidered once only with the approval of the Minister; (d) in specific cases 
of genuine difficulty, relaxation may be given allowing consideration of application even after the 
prescribed last date; and (e) except for the exceptional circumstances as above, the scheme be 
treated as closed. 
 
7.2 The Cabinet in its meeting held on March 23, 1992, considered the said Note dated 
February 27, 1992 and approved the same.  It was also decided that genuine cases of hardship 
may be looked into by the Home Minister.  However, the Supreme Court of India, in its 
judgement dated May 14, 1993, in the case of Mukund Lal Bhandari vs. Union of India (AIR 
1993 SC 2127), inter alia , directed the Government that “…the respondents should accept the 
applications of the petitioners irrespective of the date on which they are made.  The applications 
received hereafter should also be entertained w ithout raising the plea that they are beyond the 
prescribed date.”  As a result of the said decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the process of 
receipt and disposal of applications, review pe titions and filing of court cases has been unabated. 
Moreover, the closure of the Scheme had not become possible due to certain exceptions made. 
 
7.3 Many State Governments and Union Territo ry Administrations have their own schemes 
for sanction of pension to freedom fighters.  There are quite a large number of freedom fighters 
who are drawing both the State Government and Central Government pensions.  In many cases, 
where the Central Government pension has not been sanctioned, freedom fighters are receiving 
pension from the State Government, as eligibility co nditions for sanction of pension by the State 
Governments are more liberal.  Thus, eligible genuine freedom fighters are already receiving 
pension from the State Government or both from the State Government and the Central 
Government. 
 
7.4 Several instances of manipulation or forgery of documents to obtain pension have come 
to the notice of the Ministry.  In several cases,  pension was obtained on furnishing incorrect 
information or concealing material information.  Consequently, pension has been suspended in 
about 3,076 cases and cancelled in about 1,551 cases so far.  Instructions have been issued by the 
Ministry to the concerned authorities for recovery  of pension so obtained, and to prosecute the 
guilty in suitable cases. 
 
7.5 The scheme has been in operation for more than 29 years since 1972.  At present, the 
Ministry is primarily handling review petitions/M P/VIP references and court cases.  From April, 
2000 to August, 2002, out of about 23,681 review applications, including some fresh applications, 
pension has been sanctioned in only 241 cases, that  too by giving benefit of doubt in many cases.  
These exclude about 13,500 cases recommended by the Hyderabad Special Screening Committee 
from January 1997 to May 1998 and referred to the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, 
Karnataka and Maharashtra for verification.

8. Since 1972, the Government has received 6,19,277 applications from all over the country 
upto 31.8.2002 and pension has been sanctioned in 1,64,570 upto 31.8.2002.  A statement 
indicating the State-wise details is enclosed  at Annexure-III.

recommended and forwarded by the State Government, is pending with the Ministry for disposal. 
 
9.1 However, aggrieved with the decision of the Government regarding rejection of their

imprisonment. Grant of pension to all such pe ople became possible because records of their 
sufferings were available with the Central Jail, Aguada, and with the Judicial Lock up in Panaji.  
As per records, as many as 911 persons have be en granted pension on this account by this 
Ministry, and, as on date, no application, duly recommended and forwarded by the State 
Government, is pending with the Ministry. 
 
13.2 Satyagrahis of the Second Phase of the M ovement had never undergone the required six 
months of imprisonment/externment/internment et c., as required under the Scheme.  They were 
never arrested, tried and punished by the Port uguese Government and/or by the Martial Law 
Court.  They were physically thrown back from Goa into the adjoining Indian Territories in 1954-
55.  There is absolutely no record of as to how many such Satyagrahis suffered this insult of 
being thrown back primarily because no such records were ever maintained.  The Goa 
Vimochana Sahayak Samiti, Gulbarga, which has been championing the cause of freedom 
fighters of the Goa Liberation Movement and who had organized the second phase of the Goa

14. As regards pension to freedom fighters of Hyderabad Liberation Movement (1947-48),

 THE SPECIAL AUDIT TEAM (SAT)  
 
21. On August 12, 1996, during the consideration of the Demands for Grants (1996-97) of

Home Affairs that many cases received from State Governments were rejected by the Ministry 
because they lacked necessary supporting docum ents and expressed readiness to set up a

21.1 Accordingly, a Special Audit Team (SAT ) was constituted, as one time measure, on 
October 28, 1996 under the Chairmanship of the Joint Secretary incharge of the Freedom Fighters 
Division, initially for a period of three months, to review the rejected cases in which review 
applications were pending.  Two non-official s, viz., Shri Ranbir Singh, ex-MP and Working 
President of the All India Freedom Fighters Organisation, New Delhi, and Capt. S.S. Yadava, Ex-
INA and General Secretary of the All India INA Committee, New Delhi were nominated as 
members of SAT.  As per the procedure laid down, rejected cases in bundles of 50 were to be 
referred to the members for advice, and final decision was to be taken by the Joint Secretary.   
 16

 
WORK DONE BY SAT  
 
22. SAT started functioning from the month of December, 1996 and reviewed about 2000 
cases which had been rejected earlier.  A bout 800 of these cases were recommended by the 
members of SAT.  Out of the 800 cases recommended by the members of SAT, 175 cases related 
to ex-INA personnel while most of the remaining ca ses related to the State of Bihar.  Most of 
these cases were requisitioned by the members of SAT.  Some cases were also referred to the 
members, duly recommended by the Freedom Fighters’ Division of the Ministry on receipt of 
fresh information/clarification/evidence from the applicants or fresh verification/recommendation 
from the State Governments. 
  
22.1 The members of SAT recommended sanction of pension in about 700 cases straightaway, 
and in about 100 cases their recommendation was subject  to further verification or clarification 
from the concerned State Governments/applicants.  Pension has so far been sanctioned in 666 
cases.  In about 50 cases recommended by the members of SAT, it has not been found possible to 
accept their recommendations due to reasons, such as, (i) insufficiency of documentary evidence 
submitted in support of claimed suffering, (ii) lack of vital information in the documentary 
evidence regarding nature and period of claimed suffering (iii) contradiction/changes made by the 
applicants in the claimed suffering, (iv) submissi on of documents of doubtful nature, etc. and the 
same have been rejected.  
 
22.2 In the Ministry, the documentary evidence furnished by the applicants is examined 
strictly in accordance with the provisions of the Scheme and policy guidelines issued thereunder.  
However, the members of SAT adopted a more liberal approach, such as, (i) recommending cases 
on the basis of personal knowledge, (ii) giving  benefit of doubt to the applicant, (iii) 
recommending that verification/back references to  the State Government be dispensed with in 
view of advanced age, infirmity, helplessness, pove rty of the applicants, and possible delay, (iv) 
recommending the cases on the basis of personal a ffidavits of the applicants in spite of 
discrepancies in claims/records, etc.  The Mini stry alleged that most of the cases recommended 
by the members of SAT were requisitioned by th em which would indicate that they had personal 
knowledge of these cases.  The recommendation of the members of SAT was honoured in most of 
the cases. 
 
22.3 Although no formal orders were issued ex tending its tenure beyond 31.12.1996, SAT was 
allowed to function till March 1998.

25. While the information contained in the Status Note on SSSP Scheme received from 
Ministry of Home Affairs as reproduced in the pr eceding paragraphs was under consideration of 
the sub-Committee, a communication dated 8 June 2000 was received from the Ministry of Home 
Affairs regarding the proposal for the closure of the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 
1980.  The said communication delineated the following points:  
 
(i) That the scheme of political pension to freedom fighters and their eligible dependents 
known as “Freedom Fighters Pension Scheme” was introduced on 15 August, 1972 
on the occasion of 25
th anniversary of Independence; 
 
(ii) That the scheme has been in operation for almost 28 years now and pension has been 
sanctioned to 1,64,329 applicants; 
 
(iii) That out of 13,547 applications, most of which are review petitions, processed during 
the year 1999-2000, pension could be sanctioned in only 85 cases; 
 
(iv) That there are very few fresh cases; 
 
(v) That the long duration of the scheme has gi ven rise to many malpractices such as 
submission of false/forged documents, concealment of material facts, etc.   69 cases 
had to be cancelled on this account; 
 
(vi) That the scheme is a token of respect and not a quid pro quo  for the contributions 
made by the freedom fighters; 
 
(vii) That the Joint Committee of Freedom Fighter s and officials constituted to look into 
the problems of freedom fighters under the Chai rmanship of former Minister of State 
(Home) in 1997 had recommended the closure of the scheme by 31 December, 1998; 
and 
 
(viii) That many of the freedom fighters who are not eligible   for pension under the 
Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, are already receiving   pension   from   
the State Governments under their respective schemes. 
 
 18

26. In view of the aforementioned points, the Ministry proposed to discontinue the 
Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme from a prospective date after due publicity.  The 
salient features of the proposal are as follows: 
 
(a) All the State Governments will be asked to send all eligible cases pending with 
them before the said date.  The reports received by the said date in regard to 
pending cases will be duly considered. 
 
(b) Freedom fighters and their eligible dependents, who are already in receipt of 
pension, shall continue to get the same along with other facilities provided by the 
Government after closure of the scheme. 
 
(c)  Pending Court cases will also be considered after closure of the same in 
accordance with the provisions of the exis ting scheme in the light of the Court’s 
directions. 
 
27. Keeping in view the far-reaching implicati ons of the proposal of the Ministry, the sub-
Committee placed the matter before the main Committee for its consideration. 
 
27.1 The main Committee, in its meeting held on 12 September 2000, discussed at length the 
proposal of the Ministry and strongly disappr oved of the same.  The Committee unanimously 
expressed the view that the Government should continue with the scheme and asked the sub-
Committee to go ahead with the examination of th e subject assigned to it and submit its report 
thereon to it for its consideration. 
 
27.2 The sub-Committee, in its meeting held on  19 December 2001 c onsidered an updated 
Status Note received from the Ministry of Home Affairs.  The sub-Committee while recalling the 
view expressed by the main Committee in its meeting held on 12 September 2000, opined that the 
Ministry of Home Affairs should continue to operate the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension 
Scheme.  It, accordingly, decided to send its vi ews on the matter to the main Committee for its 
consideration. 
 
28. The main Committee, on the basis of the views expressed by its sub-Committee on SSSP 
Scheme, makes the following recommendations/observations vis-à-vis SSSP Scheme, 1980: 
 
(i) While strongly disapproving the proposal  of the Ministry of Home Affairs for 
closure of the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension Scheme, 1980, the Committee is 
of the considered view that the Government should continue with the operation of 
the Scheme.  The Government, however, sh ould exercise utmost care and caution so 
that no pension is sanctioned in bogus ca ses.  All applications for grant of pension 
under the scheme should be thoroughly scrutinised to ensure that pension is granted 
only in genuine cases. 
 
(ii) The Committee is also of the considered view that the Government should not close 
its doors for receiving applications from genuine freedom fighters.  It, therefore, 
urges upon the Government to dispose of  all fresh claims, if any, and review 
applications in a time bound manner as per the parameters of the Scheme.  The 
Government should also ensure that applications of genuine freedom fighters are 
processed and pension is sanctioned to them expeditiously.

REPORT
 
The Election and Other Related Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2002 (See Annexure-I) seeks to introduce State funding in kind
(supply of electoral rolls and identity slip of electors to the candidates).  It also intents to bring in transparency in the funding of
political parties  by corporate sector/any other person and to effectuate harmonisation of certain provisions in Representation of
the People Act, 1951 with Indian Panel Code 1860,  which relates to  authorisation by the candidates for meeting his/her election
expenditure by others.
 
2.0
              The Bill, therefore, proposes amendments to the following Acts: -
(i)   Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Sections 29, 39, 77, 78, 123 and 169);
(ii)  The Companies Act, 1956 (Section 293); and
(iii)The Income-Tax Act, 1961 (Sections 13 and 88)
2.1       The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill mentions that the proposed piece of legislation is an attempt to bring in

97th Report of  Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/97threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:56:47]
reforms in electoral laws in piecemeal manner in pursuance of some of the recommendations of the Committee on Electoral
Reforms (Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990), the Committee on State Funding of Elections (Indrajit Gupta Committee, 1998)
and One Hundred Seventieth Report of Law Commission of India.
 
3.0       The Bill has the following salient features: -
(a)        Limited State Funding of Elections;
(b)        Transparent system of political donations and audit & account thereof for the purpose of Income Tax
benefit to the donors; and
(c)        Harmonisation of Explanation (1) to Section 77 of Representation of the People  Act , 1951 with Section
171H of Indian Penal Code, 1860.
 
A. LIMITED STATE FUNDING OF ELECTION
 
3.1       It is a well known fact that the growing role of money and its dubious means of collection have been eroding purity and
sanctity of the election process thereby has corrupting influence  on the political system.  The central idea of State funding of
Election is to curb the corrupting   influence of money power on the electoral process by stopping the existing practice of raising
money (corporate donation and black money support) by the political parties.
 
3.2       The pattern of State funding can either be in cash or kind; it can also be total or partial.  State Funding in cash is prevalent
in certain other countries[1]
 .The issue of State funding of election in India has a chequered history[2].
 
 
3.3.0    The State funding in cash as suggested in Indrajit Gupta Committee’s Report has not seen the light of the day yet due to
lack of unanimity[3]
 amongst the States and UTs.  However, as a initial measure, the Central Government in principle has agreed
to the concept of partial State funding in kind to the recognised political parties4.
 
3.3.1    The legislation under consideration proposes to provide the following election material free of cost to the candidates set up
by the recognised parties in any General Election held for the purpose of the House of People and the Legislative Assemblies of
States-
 
(a)        Copies of electoral roll as finally published under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and such
other material as may be prescribed under the rules by the Central Government;
(b)        Identity slip of electors in the constituency concerned; and
(c)        Free airtime on electronic media.
 
3.3.2    For that purpose, a new Part VA under the caption "Free supply of certain material to candidates of recognized political
parties" divided into two Sections 78A & 78 B is proposed to be inserted5
 in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
 
 
(a)        Supply  of electoral roll of electors to the candidates.
 
3.4.0    Preparation/Revision/Correction of electoral rolls for Parliamentary/Legislative Assembly constituencies is done under the
superintendence, direction and control of Election Commission 6
, which is usually done by the Electoral Registration Officer and
Assistant Electoral Registration Officer(s).  Electoral roll of a constituency is made available to the administrative machinery
(Chief Electoral Officer, District Electoral Officer, Returning Officer, Assistant Returning Officer and Presiding Officer etc.) for
conduct of election.  But it is not made available to the candidates in the fray.  However, only two copies of electoral rolls as
finally published, are made available to those political parties for which a symbol has been exclusively reserved by the Election
Commission {section 22 (c) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960}.
 
3.4.1    As per the Bill, henceforward, copies of electoral rolls have been proposed to be made available to the candidates of the
recognized parties in the fray.
 
3.4.2    The Committee unanimously welcomed the proposal but at the same time desired that copies of electoral rolls may be
made available to the candidates of recognized parties both in hard as well as soft forms.
 
(b)        Issue of Identity slip of electors to candidates

97th Report of  Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/97threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:56:47]
 
3.5.0    Nowadays Identity slips of electors are being printed and distributed by the candidates themselves at their own expenses to
facilitate the elector to exercise his/her franchise in an effective way.
 
3.5.1    As per the provisions of the Bill, copies of Identity slip of electors would be made available to the candidates of
recognized political parties at Government's expense by the Election Commission for onward transmission to the concerned
electors.
 
3.5.2    While deliberating on the issue a point was raised in the Committee that instead of supplying Identity slip of electors to the
candidates, the same may be directly delivered to the concerned electors by the administrative machinery of the concerned
Government, which would entail saving of printing cost of multiple copies of electoral roll to be given to the candidates in the fray
and would thereby check bogus voting.
 
3.5.3    Overwhelming majority in the Committee was however of the view that supply of Identity slip of the electors to the
concerned electors by the Government would increase responsibility and expenditure, to such an extent that it would be an
horrendous task for the Government.  Further, the candidate develops good rapport with the electors in the process of distributing
such slip to the electors, which is for the benefit of the candidate.  Moreso, the representatives of the candidates remain present at
the time of polling who could identify the bogus voters.  Therefore, they were in favour of the provision for supplying such
Identity slip to the candidates instead of electors.  In that context, the Committee was of the unanimous view that issuance of
Electors photo identity card could be of great help in checking bogus voting and urged upon the Government to complete the
process of photo identity card in a time bound manner. 
 
3.5.4    The Committee in its collective wisdom considered that printing and distribution of identity slips to candidates or voters
would not be practicable and does not justify cost- benefit ratio.
 
(c)        Equitable sharing of time on electronic media
 
3.5.5    In the direction of State funding of elections, an initiative was undertaken by the Election Commission  to allow
recognised political parties to use  Government owned electronic media for propagating their manifestos.  This was done
considering the reach of the vast network of Doordarshan and All India Radio which would considerably cut down expenses of
political parties on election campaigns and general party propaganda thereby amounting to indirect State funding.
 
3.5.6    The allocation of time on State electronic media as it exists today, is available to  political parties on the basis of  the
following:
 
(i)
                  categorisation  of the political parties as National or State parties, under the provisions of the Election
Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968; and
 
(ii)
                past performance of  the political parties in the previous general election to the House of the People or State
Legislative Assemblies.
 
3.5.7    The facility is not available to unrecognised political parties or any independent candidates.  The discrimination between
recognised and unrecognised political parties for the above benefit has been treated as reasonable and valid by the Supreme Court
in the case of  Ramakant Pandey  vs. Union of India  (AIR 1993 SC 1766) and  the High Courts of Allahabad in  W.P.No.5790 of
1984 (Hari Shankar Jain vs. Chief Election Commissioner and others),  Madras in W.Ps. Nos. 12378 of 1984 and 14507 of 1989
(P.T. Srinivasan vs. Union of India and others and S. Shanmugam vs. Chief Electoral Officer, Tamil Nadu and others) and
Karnataka in W.P. No.19367 of 1984 (Raghunathmal vs. Election Commission of India and others).
 
3.5.8    National recognised parties get equitable time on both national as well as Regional Kendras of Doordarshan/All India
Radio while recognised State parties get time on Regional Kendras of Doordarshan/All India Radio for telecasting/broadcasting
their policies, programmes manifestos etc.
 
3.5.9    Allocation of time on Doordarshan/All India Radio as arranged by the Election Commission of India through its order
No.437/GE-LS/TVS/MCS/99 dated 3
rd August, 1999 is as follows:

(b)        a total of not less than 15 hours of telecasting/broadcasting time on the Regional Kendras of Doordarshan/All India
Radio by the National Parties;
 
(c)        a total of not less than 30 hours of telecasting/broadcasting time on the Regional Kendras of Doordarshan/All India
Radio by the State Parties; and
