B.         TRANSPARENT SYSTEM OF POLITICAL DONATION
 
3.6.0    Alike any other organisation, political parties too need funds for their sustenance and growth.  The parties garner resources
from different sources such as subscription fee, contribution from members and others, interest from properties of the party and
company donation, etc.  which gets deposited in the consolidated account of the party from which its expenditures are met.
 
3.6.1    Political donations as permissible under the law (Section 293A of the Companies Act, 1956) come from companies other
than Government companies.  According to Section 293A of the Companies Act, a company (other than Government company or
a company which has been in existence for less than three years) may contribute directly/indirectly  (a) to any political party (b)
for any political purpose to any person any amount not exceeding five per cent of its average net profits (taking immediately
preceding three years).  Such contribution can be made by a company only if a resolution is passed by its Board of Directors.  The
existing provision is in continuous operation7
 from 1985.
 
3.6.2    Dinesh Goswami Committee has recommended complete ban on corporate donation to political parties whereas the issue
of ban on corporate donation has been left by the Indrajit Gupta Committee to the wisdom of the Government and Parliament.
           
3.6.3    The legislation under consideration of the Committee allows 8
 political party to receive voluntary donation from the
following:
 
(a)        any company other than Government company within the stipulation of the Companies Act, 1956; and
(b)        any individual.
 
Further, donations from any foreign sources, which inter alia include a foreign company, Multi- National Company are forbidden
for this purpose.
           
3.6.4    Donation to a political party by a company has an upper limit within the stipulation of Companies Act, 1956 i.e. 5% of its
average net profit (preceding three financial years).

3.6.5    The donors (company or individual) would now be getting tax deduction on donations given to political party while
computing its/his/her total income, which has been proposed under clause 11 of the Bill9.
 
(a)        Declaration of political donation
3.6.6    The Bill intends to bring transparency in political donation for which it prescribes submission 10 of report 11 by the
treasurer of the political party containing the following items in  respect of donation received by it, to the Election Commission
before the due date for furnishing a return of its income of that financial year (substitution done by the Legislative Department in
lieu of words before the end of that financial year in the original Bill) :
 
(i)                  details of donations received from any person in that financial year;
(ii)                details of donation received from any company (other than Government company) in that financial year;
(iii)               details of expenditure incurred out of such donation; and
(iv)              a certificate regarding eligibility of donors under the law.
The political party failing to submit the aforesaid report to the Election Commission would be deprived of Income Tax relief.
           
3.6.7    As per the provision of the Bill, for transparency of accounts of donations, the report so submitted to the Election
Commission would be audited bythe Auditor approved by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India once in a financial year
to determine the expenditure on constituency campaign and expenditure on general party campaign incurred by the concerned
political party.
 
(b)        Preparation and submission of Report by Treasurer
3.7.0    As per the provisions of the Bill the treasurer of a political party will prepare and submit a report of donations received
from companies and individuals to the Election Commission, containing four items enumerated in para 3.6.6 supra.
 
3.7.1    The Committee had pointed out to the Legislative Department that there were recognized political parties, which had no
treasurer though it was mandatory for a political party to inter alia mention the name of its treasurer 12
 at the time of its
registration.  In that case any other functionary of the party, did the job of treasurer.  In that situation, the Committee felt, it would
be difficult for those parties to submit a report in the absence of its treasurer.
           
3.7.2    The Legislative Department in consultation with Election Commission has agreed to amend proposed Section 29(B) to the
effect that treasurer of a political party or any other person authorized by the political party in this behalf shall submit report to
Election Commission.
(c)        Accounting of political donation
3.8.0    While preparing the report to declare political donation received by the political parties the treasurer has to give details of
individual donors from whom the donations have been received. The upper limit  of contribution is proposed to be increased to
Rs.20,000/- by the Bill13
 above which records of the same would have to be maintained by political parties. 
 
3.8.1    The Committee observed that maintenance of list of small donors was difficult as maintenance of details of names and
addresses, etc. of individual small donors would be near to impossibility as primary party worker and others contribute in small
amount to the party.  The Committee, therefore, desired that some sort of ceiling may also be fixed for the individual donors. 
           
 
3.8.2    The Legislative Department while pointing out the proposed amendment to Section 13A of Income Tax Act, 1961 has
agreed to categorically mention the upper limit of Rs.20,000/- for maintenance of account of both the donors (companies and
individuals) for the purpose of submission of report to the Election Commission and accordingly agreed to amend clause 2
suitably.
           
3.8.3    The Committee also pointed out the difficulty arising out of issue of certificates towards the eligibility of the donors,
which was required under the Bill.  Therefore, the Committee wanted deletion of the said provision.
           
3.8.4    The Bill requires the declaration report of political donation of each party to be audited by the auditor certified by C&AG
after it is submitted to Election Commission.

3.8.5    Here it may be mentioned that under the provisions of the Bill each political party would be required to prepare and
maintain two books of accounts containing the following:-
 
(i)         all receipts and expenditure including  political donations14; and
(ii)                receipt of political donation and expenditure out of such donation exclusively.
While item (i) above is being done under the relevant provision of Income Tax Act, 1961 and is submitted to Income Tax
authorities and being audited by Chartered Accountant, as per the provision of the Bill, the report of political donation would be
submitted to Election Commission and audited by Auditors certified by the C&AG, which in turn along with audited report
thereon would be forwarded to Central Government and the latter would cause the same to be laid before each House of
Parliament. 
 
3.8.6    Many a member objected to the audit of accounts of donations by auditor approved by C&AG and its submission to
Central Government.  They were of the view that since money was not given from the public exchequer, submission of its
accounts of donation to Central Government would erode the autonomy of the political parties.  Further the auditor would have
the right to inspect any documents/premises of political parties at any point of time which was objected to on the ground that it
would tantamount to intrusion into the internal affairs of the party.  The trusts and charitable institutions, which get tax exemption,
get their accounts audited by Chartered Accountant. By subjecting the political party to get its account of donation audited by
auditor certified by C&AG would be discriminatory in the name of transparency.  The Committee unanimouslydesired that the
audit of accounts of donation received by the political party may be done through Chartered Accountants appointed by it as at
present, as per the provisions of the Income Tax Act (Section 13A).  In view thereof the Committee recommended deletion of
entire Section 29(D) in clause 2 of the Bill.
(d)        Segregation of accounts of expenditure of political party
3.9.0    The Committee pointed out that money received by political parties is deposited to a common account out of which
expenditure is incurred.  It would be difficult for the political parties to maintain different accounts for different segment of its
income, which instead of simplifying the work would increase the work of political parties without getting any substantial
benefit.  Owing to practical difficulties, the Committee did not favour the idea of maintaining two accounts in relation to
expenditure therefrom.
           
3.9.1    A section of Members wanted complete ban on corporate donation  to  political parties  as well as income tax benefit
thereon to the companies on the ground  that the companies can influence  policies of political parties.  Prevalence of corporate
donation may lead to denial of level playing  field to certain political parties. They were of the view that political parties are
becoming spokesperson of companies by receiving donations from them.  Other Members were of the view that even during the
time of ban on corporate funding, donations were received in clandestine way, which was harmful to the political system than the
present dispensation where transparency was to be maintained.   
 
C.       HARMONIZATION OF EXPLANATION TO SECTION 77 OF THE REPRESENTATION OF THE PEOPLE ACT,
1951 WITH SECTION
171 H OF INDIAN PENAL CODE, 1860
 
3.10.0  Section 171H of Indian Penal Code, 1860 expressly prohibits political parties and all other bodies/associations/individuals
to make election expenses for a candidate without his authorisation.  Whereas Explanation to Section 77 of the Representation of
the People Act, 1951 permits such expenses by others for the candidates without his authorisation.  Thus, whether the election
expenditure made by others for a candidate would be treated as part of election expenses of a candidate for the purpose of
ceiling15
 on election expenses becomes subject of interpretation due to discrepancy between relevant Sections of Indian Penal
Code, 1860 and Representation of the People Act, 1951.
 
3.10.1  The problem has arisen out of insertion of Explanation (1) to Section 77 of Representation of the People Act, 1951 in
1974.
 
3.10.2  The Supreme Court as well as Dinesh Goswami Committee had recommended restoration of Section 77 to its pre-1974
position.  The Indrajit Gupta Committee left the issue to the wisdom of the Government/Parliament.
 
3.10.3  The proposed legislation tries to harmonise both the provisions of law by substituting Explanation 1 and 3 to Section 77 of
the Representation of the People Act, 1951 by another  Explanation which clarifies that expenditure on general party campaign by
the leaders of political parties would not be treated as election expenditure by the candidate for ceiling purposes.
 
3.10.4  The numbers of leaders of recognised political party would be forty and twenty for unrecognised party for the purpose of
above benefit.
 
Segregation of security expenditure from expenditure of candidate.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The Government is continuously exploring ways and means of bringing about reforms in electoral laws with a view to
making the electoral process clean, fair and free from corrupt influences.  In this regard, the Government has before its various
recommendations made by different bodies/individuals like the Committee on Electoral Reforms  (Dinesh Goswami Committee),
the Committee on State Funding of Elections (Indrajit Gupta Committee), the Election Commission of India, the Law
Commission of India (170
th Report on Reform of Electoral Laws), etc.  The Indrajit Gupta Committee, which was constituted
pursuant to a decision taken in the all-party meeting held on 22.5.1998, considered, inter alia, the issues of State funding of
elections and other related proposals pertaining to maintenance of accounts by political parties and audit thereof, ban on donations
by companies to political parties, inclusion of expenses of political parties in the election expenses of candidates for the purposes
of ceiling on election expenses, etc., on which recommendations had been made by the Dinesh Goswami Committee in 1990.  The
Committee submitted its report to Government on 14.1.1999.  The object of the Bill is to implement some of the recommendations
of the Indrajit Gupta Committee as further considered in the light of the views expressed by the State Governments, political
parties as expressed in the all-party meeting held on 13.9.2001, Chambers of Commerce and various concerned
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government, etc.
 
2.         The Bill seeks to bring transparency in the funding of the political parties by the corporate sector and by other persons by
streamlining and promoting the donations received by the political parties for elections by giving suitable tax-exemptions and
withdrawal thereof in specified circumstances.  In this connection, it may be stated that section 293A inserted in the Companies
Act, 1956 in 1960 provided for contribution by the companies to the political parties.  After severe  criticism of the role of money
power in the politics, the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1969 prohibited  making of political contributions and also made it
punishable.  Section 293A was again amended in 1985 allowing the corporate sector to play its legitimate role in the functioning
of the Indian democracy, within the defined norms.  The Dinesh Goswami Committee was of the considered view that the
donations made by companies to political parties be completely banned.  However, the Indrajit Gupta Committee left the decision
in this regard to the wisdom of Parliament and the Government.  The corrupting influence of money in politics has, however, not
abated despite these legislative remedies.
 
3.         The Bill also seeks to address the problems arising out of insertion of Explanation 1 to section 77(1) of the Representation
of the People Act, 1951 which permits political parties and all other bodies or associations or individuals to make election
expenses for a candidate without his authorisation.  Explanation 3 thereto is also sought to be deleted.
 
4.         The Bill further seeks to make provisions for allocation of equitable sharing of time on the cable television network and
other electronic media for the purposes of election campaign as well as State funding in kind in respect of supply of free copies of
electoral rolls to the candidates by the Government and for supply of identity slips of electors and other prescribed items by the
Election Commission to the candidates.
 
4.
      The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
 
            Clause 3 of the Bill seeks to insert section 39A after section 39 in the Representation of the People Act, 1951.  The
proposed section 39A relates to allocation of equitable sharing of time for the purposes of election campaign.  The time shall be
allocated in the prescribed manner on the cable television network and other electronic media.  The electronic media includes
radio and any other broadcasting media notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette.  This may involve costs for
the Government owned or controlled media.
 
2.         Clause 5 of the Bill seeks to insert new Part VA in the Representation of the People Act, 1951 relating to partial State
funding in kind.  The proposed section 78A relates to the free supply of copies of electoral rolls, as finally published under the
Representation of the People Act, 1950, to the candidates by the Government.  The proposed section 78B provides for supply of
identity slips of electors and other prescribed items by the Election Commission to the candidates.
 
3.         The Bill, if enacted, would involve annual recurring expenditure and a non-recurring expenditure from the Consolidated
Fund of India.  It is, however, not possible to calculate the estimate of the expenditure involved in the purported measures as it is
not possible to anticipate with any accuracy the number of contestants in an election as well as the number of voters in any
constituency in view of the continuous change in their numbers on various accounts.
 
MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
 
Clause 7 of the Bill seeks to amend section 169 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 by inserting clauses (aa), (bb),  (hh)
and (hhh) after clauses (a), (b) and (h) respectively in sub-section (2) thereof.  The proposed clauses (aa), (bb),  (hh) and (hhh)
empower the Central Government to make rules to provide for the form of donation report, the manner of allocation of equitable
sharing of time on the cable television network and other electronic media, the material to be supplied by the Government to the
candidates of recognised political parties at any general election held for the purposes of constituting the House of the People or
the Legislative Assembly of a State and the items to be supplied by the Election Commission to the candidates set up by the
recognised  political parties respectively.
 
2.

No. 437/GE-LS/TVS/MCS/99                                                            Dated: August 03, 1999
 
Telecast/Broadcast facility to political parties during elections
 
ORDER
 
At the time of General Elections to the Lok Sabha in February, 1998 the Election Commission of India had taken up a new
initiative for State funding of recognized political parties through free use of State owned Television and Radio under directions
of the Commission (Vide Order No. ECI/GE98/437/MCS/98 dated 16th January 1998).
2.         The scheme was discussed in detail with representatives of all National and State recognized political parties on the eve of
the Lok Sabha Elections in 1998.  All the Parties welcomed the proposal of the Election Commission.  The Commission in
comprehensive consultations with the Prasar Bharati Corporation.  Doordarshan and All India Radio gave the operational
parameters of the scheme.
3.         The recognized National and State political parties were allotted 122 hours for telecast/broadcast over DD/AIR in the new
scheme.  The concept of time vouchers for parties was also introduced at that time.  The Scheme proved to be very useful and was
much appreciated particularly because it provided for State funding in a manner which could not be misused.
4.         The Commission, subsequently successfully extended the said scheme to the General Elections to the legislative
assemblies of 4 States, namely, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Rajasthan and NCT of Delhi, held in November, 1998 and State of
Goa in June, 1999.
5.         The Commission is determined to carry forward this scheme and expand its scope.  Accordingly, the Commission has now
decided to extend the said scheme to the ensuing General Elections to Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies of certain States,
1999.
6.         Accordingly, the Commission after consultation with the Prasar Bharati Corporation, and in exercise of its plenary powers
of superintendence, direction and control, inter alia of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures vested in it by Article 324 of
the Constitution of India, nereby directs, as follow:

6.0       The Secretary thanked the Committee for the opportunity given to him to make a presentation.  He made some
observations on the position obtaining in some other countries of the world on such matters as public funding, private
contributions and tax deductibility of donations made to the political parties.
 
6.1       Touching upon the issue of funding of parties he stated that there was no uniform practice the world over.  He said that in
Australia and Canada the practice was of post-election funding of political parties, whereas in Israel funds were given to political
parties during the election period.  In New Zealand and South Africa funds were given to the parties at the end of every financial
year.  He further stated that anonymous contributions were prohibited by most of the countries.  While Germany laid down a limit
beyond which donations were prohibited if the donor could not be identified and further the donations exceeding the specified
limit were to be reported, in USA all contributions were to be recorded but donations exceeding the specified limits must be
disclosed.

12.       Demand Nos. 93, 94, 95, 96 and 97 which are given in Volume-II of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of
Home Affairs, relate to Union Territories (without Legislature), namely Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra
& Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep, respectively. The entire budget of the Union Territories (without
Legislature) on the Plan as well as Non-Plan side is reflected in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry. Though the budget
of these Union Territories forms part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, being the nodal Ministry, it, however, does not dilute
the responsibilities of the Ministries of the Central Government from scrutinising and sanctioning the schemes under their
purview. The factual position regarding budgetary procedure in this regard is that the entire budget requirement for Plan
and Non-Plan, revised estimates for current year and Non-Plan budget estimates for the ensuing year is discussed by the
Ministry of Finance in the pre-budget meetings with the representatives of the concerned Union Territories and Ministry of
Home Affairs. An overall ceiling is fixed in respect of each Union Territory. The Planning Commission decides annual
Plan allocations for the ensuing year. The Union Territory Administrations prepare budgetary break-up showing budget
provisions according to their respective budgetary heads and also showing the allocation against Ministries/Departments of
the Central Government administratively concerned. This budgetary break-up is included in the Demands for Grants of the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
PRESENTATION OF HOME SECRETARY ON DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2002-2003)
13.       The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in its meetings held on 20, 21, 24 and 25 March
2003.  The Home Secretary made a power-point presentation before the Committee on 21 March 2003.
14.       The Home Secretary began his presentation with an overview of internal security situation in the country.  He
apprised the Committee of the progress made on various fronts and the steps and measures taken during 2002-2003.  He
stated that living in a unipolar world with a few nation states deciding the course of action anywhere in the globe, as
evidenced by the war on Iraq which began recently, was difficult. The alliance against terrorism which was formed
subsequent to September 11, 2001 attacks on the World Trade Centre and Pentagon, had given way to an alliance of powers
based on their own perceptions of what was good for the world and in the process, the multilateralism of the UN
mechanism had been marginalized and bypassed.  This had implications for our internal security inasmuch as the
perception that Pakistan was cooperating in the war against terrorism was masking, for the powers that be, the fact that it
was also a breeding ground for Jihadi  terrorism.  Though India's position regarding Pakistan sponsored terrorism was
accepted in the international fora, for short-term gains, this reality was being papered over.  The Home Secretary

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
emphasized that it would be, therefore, realistic to say that India had to fight against cross-border terrorism on its own. He
further mentioned that during the course of the year, there had been no let up in terrorist activities.  During the course of last
12 months, there were a number of major events of terrorist strike such as attack on Raghunath Mandir in March and
November, 2002, Killings at Kaluchak in Jammu in April, 2002, attack on Akashardham Mandir, Gandhinagar in
September, 2002, attack on Amarnath Yatris in August, 2002,Mumbai bomb blasts in a bus at Ghatkopar in December,
2002, and  bomb blasts in a local train at Mulund in March, 2003 in Mumbai.
 
14.1     He further stated that given the geo-political scenario, the continued reliance of the U.S. on Pakistan and Pakistan’s
own domestic compulsions would mean that there would be no immediate respite from cross-border terrorism primarily in
Jammu & Kashmir but aided and abetted elsewhere also in the country.  He believed that eternal vigilance, therefore, would
have to be the order of the day.
           
15.       Thereafter, the Home Secretary gave a detailed description of the internal security trends in vulnerable and sensitive
parts of the country.
 
16.       With regard to the situation in Jammu & Kashmir, the Home Secretary stated  that the promise made by President
Musharraf of Pakistan in January 2002 on the issue of cross-border terrorism remained unfulfilled.  The releasing of chiefs
of terrorist outfits like LeT and JeM by Pakistan Government proved beyond doubt its nefarious designs and double speak.
Hence, the Union Government was pursuing a multi-pronged strategy to bring peace & normalcy in the State which
comprised tackling cross border terrorism, accelerated economic development and dialogue with people/groups of J&K
who eschewed the path of violence.  He stated that as part of mobilizing public opinion against terrorism, the democratic
structure was strengthened in the State by holding Panchayat elections after 24 years and free and fair Assembly elections
with large voter turnouts.  He placed before the Committee the statistics relating to terrorist violence in the State during
2002 and stated that 453 security forces personnel were killed as compared to 536 in 2001, 255 explosions took place as
compared to 402 in 2001 whereas the number of terrorists killed was 1707 as compared to 2020 in 2001 out of which as
many as 508 were foreign mercenaries.  He hoped that the trend of decline in those figures registered after 2001, would
continue to be maintained over the next few years. He observed that Pakistan had not stopped using cross-border infiltration
as tactical tool for fomenting terrorist violence in Jammu and Kashmir despite the diplomatic pressure exerted by the world
community.
 
16.1     The Home Secretary drew the attention to the fact that terrorist attacks were clearly directed against Government
establishment and security establishments and security forces with more emphasis on Fidayeen  or suicide attacks. He
stressed that terrorists responsible for Fidayeen  attacks were all Pakistanis. He went on to emphasise that terrorists were
aided and abetted by the forces across the border through the help in the form of arms and ammunitions as well as finances.
He, however, mentioned that Fidayeen or suicide attacks declined to 10 in 2002 from 28 in 2001.    Further, he stated that
terrorist activities remained unabated notwithstanding the PDP-Congress combine Government’s sympathetic gesture.  He
informed that a Standing Committee headed by Cabinet Secretary had been constituted to monitor the development
programmes of the Central Ministries in the State.  He also referred to infrastructural development projects for the State
announced by the Prime Minister during his visit in May 2002 and stated that the financial outlay on these schemes/projects
would be to the tune of Rs. 6000 crore.  Besides, he mentioned the appointment of Shri N.N. Vohra as an interlocutor to
carry forward dialogue with elected representatives and   informed that he had already begun his work.
 
17.       While apprising the Committee of the situation in North-East, the Home Secretary stated that the level of violence in
the region had declined, though the internal security situation particularly in Nagaland, Assam, Manipur and Tripura needed
to be handled with sensitivity and urgency. He enumerated various outfits active in those States and observed that presence
of long porous border and various inhospitable terrains coupled with inflow of illegal arms and influx of illegal migrants
had facilitated the growth and movement of militant groups. In addition, lack of economic development and employment
opportunity, and assistance from Pak ISI were also contributing to the growth of militancy in the region.  While giving
details of the terrorist violence in the region, the Home Secretary stated that during the year 2002, there were 1312 incidents
of violence compared with 1338 incidents in 2001. During 2002, 457 civilians and 147 security personnel were killed in
terrorist violence as against the figures of 600 civilians and 175 security personnel during 2001. Similarly 571 militants
were killed in 2002 compared to 572 killed the year before. Arms looted by militants were 87 in 2002 as compared to 111
in 2001. The number of arms recovered was 610 in 2002 as compared to 577 in 2001. He stated that the statistics proved
that the number of extremist related incidents came down along with the decline in losses of life of civilians as well as
security personnel.  On the other hand the recovery of arms increased and the number of extremists killed remained the

same. Further, he expected that with the peace initiative taken by the Government the extremist related violence would
substantially go down.
 
17.1     The Home Secretary informed that the number of items to be reimbursed under the scheme of Security Related
Expenditure was expanded substantially. Besides, Ministry of Home Affairs was also implementing a 100% centrally
funded scheme i.e. “Scheme of Special Central Assistance in Kind” to the North Eastern States for modernisation of their
police forces.  The Ministry had also sanctioned 24 India Reserve Battalions to the North Eastern States including Sikkim
(2 each for Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland; 6 for Assam, 4 for Manipur, 5 for Tripura and 1 for
Sikkim) with the objective to reduce the dependence of States on CPMFs. Referring to the peaceful and successful
conclusion of Assembly elections in Nagaland, Tripura and Meghalaya, held in February 2003, the Home Secretary stated
that adequate CPMFs were made available to the State Governments for that purpose.
 
17.2     Further elaborating upon the peace initiatives taken by the Government in the North-Eastern region, the Home
Secretary informed that the formal ceasefire between Government of India and NSCN (I-M) group of Nagaland had been
extended upto 31 July, 2003.  The ban under Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 on NSCN (I-M) was not renewed
after 26 November 2002 to facilitate holding of peace talks in India during January 2003.  After the talks were held in
February 2003, an understanding had been reached for continuation of formal talks until a lasting settlement was reached. 
Meanwhile, both sides reaffirmed the need for a peaceful and violence free environment.  The Government had also entered
into a formal ceasefire with NSCN (K) group which had been extended up to 28 April, 2003.  With a view to make the
ceasefire effective, ground rules were formulated to enforce the ceasefire between the security forces, NSCN (I-M) and
NSCN (K).  Ceasefire Monitoring Group and Cease Fire Supervisory Board had been set up for enforcing ground rules in
respect of NSCN (I-M) and NSCN (K), respectively. 
 
17.3     While making a mention of the Memorandum of Settlement signed between the Central Government, the
Government of Assam and Bodo-Liberation Tigers (BLT) on 10 February, 2003 for durable solution to the Bodo issue, the
Home Secretary stated that it had been agreed to create the Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) within the State of Assam
and under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India.  Adequate safeguards had been built-up for the interests of non-
tribals in the BTC area.  The Government had also agreed to consider favourably the inclusion of Bodo language in the
Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.  Besides, it would also be the official language of BTC along with Assamese and
English.  He stated that Government would provide Rs. 100 crore per annum for 5 years for socio-economic and
infrastructure development of BTC area over & above the normal plan assistance to Assam.  The Government would also
fund a Central Institute of Technology to impart education in technical and vocational disciplines.  Initiatives had also been
taken for peace dialogue with various other militant bodies viz. NSCN-K, United Peoples Democratic Solidarity (UPDS)
and Dima Halam Daogah (DHD).  The ceasefire with DHD was effective from 1 January 2003 for six months, whereas, the
ceasefire with UPDS was effective from 1August 2002 for a year.
 
17.4     The Home Secretary while sharing his concern with the Committee stated that the worrying feature of the North
Eastern militancy had been the trans-national linkages of some of the groups for the purpose of procurement of arms and
ammunition, especially with ISI of Pakistan and other inter-group relations within North-East.  The Government was also
concerned about existence of Indian insurgent camps in neighbouring countries namely, Bangladesh, Myanmar, and
Bhutan.  The matter had been taken up with the Governments of these countries who assured that they would not allow
undesirable elements to use their territory for activities prejudicial to the interest of India.
 
18.       With regard to left wing extremism, the Home Secretary stated that the magnitude as well as the intensity of left
wing extremist violence registered an upsurge  during 2002 which witnessed 1465 incidents and 482 deaths as compared to
1208 incidents and 564 deaths in 2001. Besides, 121 extremists were killed, 537 arms recovered, 2523 extremists arrested
and 691 surrendered following the police action.  Although a comparison of the statistics revealed that the number of
extremists arrested as well as surrendered had gone up, the left wing extremist influence witnessed a considerable
geographical spread with new areas coming under its influence.  The entire left wing movement spread over 53 districts in 9
States.  Apart from traditional strongholds of the movement, its newly acquired areas of influence were Chattisgarh,
Western districts of West Bengal, parts of North Bihar, Eastern UP and Eastern as well as Southern Jharkhand.  For the first
time, Jharkhand emerged as the worst affected in terms of quantum of violence overtaking Andhra  Pradesh.  While in
Andhra  Pradesh naxalite violence was lower primarily on account of extended periods of unilateral ceasefire and over 7

months ‘strategic restraint’ of the CPML-PW, the outfit made substantial gains by way of large scale extortions and
substantial recruitment of armed cadres.  Chattisgarh also emerged as a major cause for concern as the left wing extremist
violence nearly doubled in the State surpassing even Bihar and became the third most affected State.  The expansionist
design of the CPML-PW was discernible in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala.  The Home Secretary stated that the
Compact Revolutionary Zone (CRZ) envisaged by the MCC, the CPML-PW and the CPN (Maoist) for linking up the
strongholds of the CPML-PW in Telengana and Dandkaranya regions and of the MCC in Bihar and Jharkhand with those of
the CPN (Maoist) in Nepal by cutting across Chhattisgarh, continued to be a live concern.   Among other worrisome
developments were the rapid increase in the front of militarisation of armed formation, use of GF rifles and bullet proof
jackets, usage of remote controls and timer devices, significant induction of new armed recruits and increase in the military
training camps.  Besides, left wing extremists continued to hold Jan Adalats and indulge in extortions in their strongholds. 
 
18.1     Further, while speaking on the strategy to tackle Left Wing Extremism the Home Secretary stated that the
Coordination Centre set up to deal with the problem concentrated on both the security and developmental aspects.  It
reviewed the existing and emerging security scenario from time to time and modified the strategy accordingly.  In the latest
meeting of the Coordination Centre, held on 8 November 2002 at Ranchi and a meeting of Union Home Secretary with
Chief Secretary of Chattisgarh held on 16 January 2003 at Raipur, the affected States were asked to plan an integrated
approach towards the Left Wing Extremism including modernisation and strengthening of the State Police forces and its
intelligence branches, their police networks and providing sophisticated arms and communication system, prevention of Jan
Adalats and gearing up  the judicial system for speedy disposal of criminal and civil matters.  There was also need for
coordinated action amongst the affected States, effective governance and proper training inputs for the State Police forces. 
Referring to the discussion on the issue in Chief Minister’s Conference held on 8 February 2003, he stated that it was
agreed to have a well-focused strategy to check, resolve and reorient towards Left Wing Extremism which included
pursuing a number of specially directed policies such as strengthening and modernization of State police forces, better
training to police personnel, strategic planning, special task forces for anti-naxalite operations, etc.  The affected States
were also advised to pay attention to developmental aspects, gear up their grievance redressal system at the grassroot level
so that justice was neither denied nor delayed.  The Conference also emphasized upon the need for good governance and
need to make the administrative machinery more responsive, sensitive and transparent.  The Home Secretary informed the
Committee that an   additional grant of Rs.96.70 crore in the form of 'Security Related Expenditure' was sanctioned to the
affected States.  14 India Reserve Battalions in the 9 Left Wing Extremism affected States had already been sanctioned
whereas the need for 5 more IR battalions in such States was discussed with the Finance Ministry.  The Ministry of Home
Affairs also requested the Planning Commission to include 53 LWE affected districts under their new scheme, ‘Backward
Districts Initiative’, providing an additional sum of Rs.15 crore per year per district.  Besides, the Deputy Prime Minister
had also asked the Finance Minister to arrange for sanctioning an additional amount of Rs.2385 crore to the Planning
Commission over and above its normal gross-budgetary support for next three years for the affected districts specifically
earmarked for 'Backward Districts Initiative'. 
 
19.       In relation to the situation in Punjab, the Home Secretary stated that the law and order situation in Punjab on
militancy front remained, by and large, under control during 2002.  Security forces arrested 29 extremists and 3 extremists
surrendered in 2002 as against 37 arrested and one surrendered in 2001. However, the worrisome feature was the recovery
of high explosives and arms & ammunition including AK rifles, grenades and RDX.  Pakistan had been continuously
providing sanctuary to militant groups such as Khalistan Commando Force, Babbar Khalsa International (BKI), Khalistan
Zindabad Force and International Sikh Youth Federation (ISYF), which were banned under POTA, 2002. Among these 
BKI and ISFY had been even banned under UK Terrorism Act, 2000.  They were included in the list of terrorist
organizations by the European Union also.  Pakistan was also engaged in a propaganda aimed at driving a wedge between
Hindus and Sikhs.  The top Sikh extremist leaders continued to find security and financial assistance from Pakistan. 
Pakistan was also engaged in development of nexus between the Sikh and Kashmiri terrorist groups.  He submitted that the
Ministry of Home Affairs was keeping a close watch on the situation.
 
20.       Touching upon the situation in the capital city of Delhi, the Home Secretary informed that the capital’s crime graph
had shown a consistent increase till 1998 and started showing declining trend in 1999. This downward trend continued
during 2002 also. Besides, Delhi Police had in the last two years achieved significant successes in controlling the activities
of various terrorist organizations, inter-state gangsters and the Mumbai underworld in Delhi. During 2002, Delhi Police
arrested or killed 46 terrorists belonging to JKLF, Al Qaieda, Harkat-ul-Jehad-e-Islami, Hizbul Muzahideen, SIMI,
Lashkar-e-Toiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad whereas in 2001 it arrested or killed 58 militants, thus containing their activities

in Delhi. Besides, no incident of bomb blast was reported in 2002 as compared to three such incidents in 2001.  Special
security arrangements in the highly sensitive areas covering important Government buildings like Rashtrapati Bhawan,
Parliament House, Parliament House Annexe, Prime Minister’s Office and residence, North and South Blocks, Defence
Headquarters and others were also put in place.  In order to strengthen security in the areas inhabited by the Members of

purchase of vehicles at an expenditure of more than Rs.2 crore.  In addition many steps had been taken to modernize the

unit, etc.
 
21.       Touching upon the activities of Pak ISI, the Home Secretary stated that Pakistan had consistently used terrorism and
covert action as an instrument of State policy against India.  It provided sanctuary to known anti-India elements and those
declared as fugitives from the law in India.  Pakistan was also focusing its attention to Nepal and Bangladesh as its major
launching bases for anti-India operations.  He informed that a comprehensive pro-active strategy to counter Pak ISI
activities was being developed in the Ministry.     In order to neutralise ISI agents, the Central Government had adopted a
well coordinated and multi-pronged approach which included strengthening the border management, gearing up of
intelligence machinery, well coordinated intelligence based action against ISI agents and militants sponsored by them and
modernisation and upgradation of police and security forces with advanced sophisticated weapons and communication
system, etc.  As a result of the coordinated efforts by the Central and State Agencies, 110 ISI backed modules and 71
espionage modules had been neutralised in various States during the last three years.
 
21.1     In relation to communal violence, the Home Secretary stated that except for the Godhra incident and its fall out, the
communal situation in the country remained by and large under control during 2002. The year registered 671 communal
incidents in which 1126 persons got killed and 4138 injured as compared to 778 incidents involving 210 deaths and 2174
injuries in 2001. These figures included the casualties during the major communal riots which took place in Gujarat
following the Godhra train carnage on 27 February 2002.  Thus both number of incidents as also the casualties came down
during the year except the unfortunate incidents of Gujarat.  He informed that nearly 90% of the communal incidents were
reported from 11 States, namely, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal,
Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Jharkhand and Tamil Nadu.  The majority of reported incidents were due to trivial and non-
religious issues. He submitted that the Government was alive to the efforts being made to escalate tension between
communities and was maintaining a close watch over the situation. The incidents of attack on the Christians & Christian
institutions too showed a downward trend during 2002 as compared to 2001.   Tamil Nadu reported the maximum number
of incidents followed by Orissa, Kerala and Maharashtra.
 
22.       Referring to the caste related incidents, the Home Secretary stated that the number of such incidents and persons
killed in caste violence in 2002 declined by 6% and 45%, respectively as compared to 2001.  Tamil Nadu reported
maximum number of incidents followed by Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Regional tensions too remained
under control. The agitational activities for the demand of creation of separate Telangana State, Harit Pradesh, Kisan
Pradesh, Poorvanchal Pradesh, Bundelkhand and Central Uttar Pradesh remained on a low during the year. The demands
for a separate State of Gorkhaland and Kamptapur had been raised. About agrarian unrest, he stated that it remained by and
large peaceful during 2002. The incidents which took place on this front could be attributed to the demands such as
advanced fixation of minimum support price for agricultural produce, higher price for sugarcane, adequate compensation to
drought hit farmers, release of irrigation water, adequate water supply, free electricity, etc.  Similarly, the law and order
situation on the labour front also by and large remained calm during 2002 in sharp contrast to the situation experienced
during 2001.  The significant decline in strikes/agitations was attributed to strong determination of the Government to go
ahead with the reform programmes.

floodlighting works in Punjab and Rajasthan sectors were satisfactory. The total length of the border to be fenced was

Left Wing Extremism
 
41.       Left wing extremism is proving to be a serious challenge to the internal security of the country.  In 2002, a sudden
spurt has been witnessed in the level of violence by left wing extremists.  During the year, 1465 incidents of violence have
been reported as against 1208 incidents in 2001.  Today, its tentacles have spread to new areas also such as North
Chattisgarh, Western districts of West Bengal, parts of North Bihar, Eastern UP and Eastern and Southern Jharkhand.  In
all, 53 districts in 9 States of the country are under the sway of this movement.  The Government of India along with the
Governments of the affected States has been adopting a two pronged strategy which aims at neutralizing the cadres of the
extremist outfits, PWG and MCC and at the same time focusing its attention on developmental activities in the affected
areas.  A number of steps have been taken on the law & order front to control the situation.  On economic and development
front, the Ministry of Home Affairs has sent a proposal to the Planning Commission for the inclusion of these 53 affected
districts in its new scheme ‘Backward Districts Initiative’ so that additional funds are earmarked to remove their socio-
economic backwardness as per this scheme.  This apart, moves are afoot to ensure good governance and make the
administrative machinery more responsive, sensitive and transparent in the affected areas.  Effective public grievances
redressal system is also proposed to be put in place.
 
41.1     The strategy being adopted by the affected States with the assistance of the Union Government does not seem to be
yielding desired results.  Although the Government can always claim success of its strategy by furnishing figures of the
extremists killed, arrested and surrendered, the bottom line is that this problem is gradually spiralling.  The growth and
spread of the movement may be attributed to its growing clout amongst the common people.  The extremists appear to have
apparently been able to strike the right chord with the people as they have been successful in convincing a section of the
people that the State and its machinery are mainly responsible for all their woes.  This is precisely the reason for a complete
drought of intelligence inputs from the people living in affected areas.  People appear to prefer extremists over the police
and other Government agencies when it comes to making a choice between the two.  It is unfortunate that people like the
extremists, are also losing faith in the State.  Therefore, the need of the hour is to restore people’s faith in the State and its
agencies.  To the contrary, the focus of the strategy to tackle the problem appears to be more on dealing with it purely as a
law and order problem than on striking at its socio-economic roots.  As a matter of fact, no serious efforts have so far been
made to go into the socio-economic causes of the problem with a view to find a lasting solution to it.  Innocent people are
caught between the extremists and the law enforcement agencies and thus are victims at the hands of both.  On the one
hand, people are forced, at gun point, to provide food and shelter to ultras and on the other, they are subjected to harassment

Modernisation of State Police Forces
 
42.       Police is synonymous with Government. Hence its strength and efficiency should always be upto the mark for
continuance of a Government especially a democratic one.  Keeping this in mind the Central Government took up police
modernization plan in late 1960s.  The Ministry of Home Affairs has been implementing a Non-plan Scheme for
Modernisation of State Police Forces since 1969-70 on a 50:50 cost sharing basis.  However, during the period 1969-70 to
1999-2000, a total amount of Rs.536.74 crore has been released to various State Governments on account of this scheme
which is in real terms a meager sum for such a vast project.  In view of the emerging challenges and threats to the internal
security, particularly in the form of extremism, terrorism and religious fundamentalism including left-wing extremism in
some parts of the country, the annual Central allocation under the Scheme for Modernisation of the State Police Forces was
enhanced to Rs.1000 crore from 2000-01 for 10 years.  Nevertheless, the sum allocated for 2000-01 & 2001-02 could be
utilised to the extent of 71% and 43%, respectively.
 
 42.1    The Ministry replying to a question mentioned that the Scheme provides for review of implementation after every
two years.  Accordingly, a Review Committee was constituted under a Special Secretary of Ministry of Home Affairs.  The
Committee visited a few major States and observed implementation of the Scheme.  The views of the State Governments
were also obtained regarding various aspects of the Scheme.  Most of the State Governments have expressed their inability
to contribute matching share due to financial constraints as per the underlying principle of the Scheme.  The Committee
submitted its report on implementation of the scheme.  It has inter alia recommended that the funding pattern of the
Scheme needs to be changed whereby Central Government’s share should be increased to 75% out of which 50% should be

in the form of grant-in-aid and 25% as loan. 
 
42.2     The Home Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on Demands for Grants (2003-04) stated that the
Central Government had been regularly reminding the States in Chief Ministers’ Conferences and through letters to the
Chief Secretaries of States, to send perspective action plans for modernisation of their Police Forces. However, the States
have been found wanting in utilising the allotted funds.  The lack of initiative on the part of a majority of States is
apparently due to their inability to spare requisite matching funds.  This has led to a situation where the Union Government
is keen to modernise the State police forces but State Governments are not too keen to implement the scheme meant for the
purpose owing to paucity of financial resources at their disposal.  This peculiar situation emanates, to a large extent, from
the federal structure of our polity.  As per the constitutional framework, the subjects of ‘Police’ and ‘Public order’ fall
within the jurisdiction of State Governments whereas the overall responsibility for maintenance of internal security has
been vested with the Union Government under Article 355.  Accordingly, creation, maintenance and supervision of police
forces including their augmentation and modernisation are the primary responsibility of the State Governments.  Therefore,
States are duty bound to ensure that their police forces are fully equipped to meet the challenges being posed on the law and
order front.  As far as maintenance of internal security is concerned, it is the Union Government which has been enjoined
upon by the Constitution to maintain it.  Thus, the founding fathers of the Constitution tried to draw a distinct line between
the jurisdiction and responsibilities of the two Governments.   However, in practice, this line has proved to be very thin and
more often than not, it has completely blurred or vanished.  This is so because what is seen as a threat to law and order also
has a direct bearing on overall internal security and vice versa.  Thus, law and order and internal security are closely
intertwined with each other.  A change in one also gets reflected in the other.  It is precisely the reason why Ministry of
Home Affairs launched a scheme for the modernisation of State police forces as it fully realized that unless the machinery
for maintenance of law & order was strengthened, it would not be able to maintain a foolproof internal security.  Now the
question arises as to why State Governments are not paying as much attention as needed to modernize their police forces? 
Why modernisation of police is not being taken up on priority by the States even though they are fully aware of the dangers
to the general law & order situation?  Here, it may be pointed out that when it comes to the control and superintendence of
police forces, the States do not want to yield even an inch of their jurisdiction.  But at the same time when it comes to
improve and strengthen their police forces, they simply raise their hands expressing their inability to do so because of
financial constraints.  The height is that most of them are not even prepared to meet half of the expenses as per the scheme
of the Union Government.  Given the situation, the Union Government must make some earnest efforts to ensure the active
participation of State Governments in modernising their police forces.  The Union Government should not have a feeling of
helplessness in convincing the State Governments to focus their attention on this issue.  After all, Article 355 places the
responsibility of protecting the States from internal disturbances on the shoulders of the Union Government.  Therefore, the
Union Government will be well within its rights if it issues necessary instructions to the State Governments to come
forward and join it in modernising their police forces in the larger interest of maintaining internal security.  Undoubtedly,
the States have to pull up their socks and exercise financial prudence so as to spare requisite funds for implementation of
the scheme.
 
42.3     The Committee while realising the importance of the role of the State Governments in modernising their police
forces is also conscious of the poor financial position of the States.  Keeping that in view it endorses the proposal which
envisages a new funding pattern based on 75:25 ratio.  This new pattern will reduce the liability of the States from present
50% to 25% of the funds to be used for the modernisation of State police forces.  Here a genuine concern arises as to what
if State Governments fail to provide even half of what they are required to provide at present.  It once again takes the
Committee back to its conclusion mentioned in the preceding paragraphs that States will have to find ways and means to
provide their share of the requisite funds.  The State Governments just cannot afford to look up to the Union Government. 
In a nutshell, the Committee while recommending a switchover to the new funding pattern of 75:25 for implementation of
the scheme, is also of the view that the Union Government should evolve a suitable mechanism to seek active participation
of State Governments in its efforts to modernise their police forces.
 
42.4     The Government of India may also consider the possibility of earmarking the States’ share for modernisation of
police forces while providing annual central plan assistance to them so as to ensure the effective participation of the States
in the implementation of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces.  The Government may further consider to
stop the release of funds so earmarked in central plan assistance in respect of States who are found wanting vis-à-vis the
implementation of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces.
 
42.5     Another issue related to the scheme for modernisation of State police forces is the monitoring of the implementation
of this scheme and the assessment of the actual benefits of the scheme accrued to the States. There has always been an
element of doubt over the actual benefits that accrue to the States out of a centrally sponsored scheme because the actual

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
implementation of the scheme rests with the concerned State Governments. Although there is a provision for review of the
implementation of the scheme by Ministry of Home Affairs after every two years, there is no credible information available
to assess the actual benefits. All that is available is the details of the funds allocated to various States over the years.
Moreover, the periodic review done in two years’ time is more of a routine bureaucratic exercise. Therefore, the need of the
hour is that a specialised central agency should be entrusted with the task to oversee the implementation of this scheme. It is
the Committee’s considered view that there can be no better agency than BPR&D to be entrusted with this task. BPR&D
has the expertise and experience to take upon itself this responsibility. All that it requires is necessary manpower and
wherewithal to perform this duty. By entrusting this task to the BPR&D, a constant, regular and effective monitoring of the
scheme can be ensured which will bring about a sea change in the way this scheme is being implemented and monitored at
present.  The Committee is also of the view that it should be made mandatory for BPR&D to submit quarterly status reports
in respect of the beneficiary States vis-à-vis the implementation of this scheme.
 
42.6     Another aspect of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces which needs a re-look is the question as to
whether the present scheme of allotting funds to the State Governments should continue or it should be replaced by a
scheme whereby the central assistance is given in kind and not in cash as it is being done in the case of North-Eastern
States.  Here it may again be worth mentioning that the real benefits of centrally sponsosred schemes fail to reach the
intended beneficiaries quite often than not as a result of which the purpose behind a scheme gets defeated.  Keeping this
view in mind, it is felt that whatever assistance is to be extended to the States it should be in kind and not in cash.  There are
a couple of benefits of following this policy.  One, uniformity in providing standard equipments/gadgets can be ensured to
all the States.  Second, the apprehensions regarding misutilisation of allotted funds can be removed.  Third, the speedy
implementation of a scheme can be ensured if equipment/gadgets are procured at the central level and made available to the
States directly thereby doing away with the usual cumbersome cycle starting from allocation of funds to the final
procurement and installation of equipment/gadgets.
 
42.7     In case of the scheme for modernisation of State police forces, there are two aspects.  One, it aims at improving the
physical infrastructure such as police stations, police posts, buildings, etc.  And the other is the provision of modern
weaponry, equipment, gadgetry, computers, etc. to the police forces to improve their strike capability and general
functioning.  As far as the first aspect is concerned, the present scheme involving release of funds needs no change for
obvious reasons.  It is the second aspect, which happens to be crucial from the point of view of improving the strike
capability of the police forces, that needs a shift from cash to kind.  The Committee is of the view that under the scheme for
modernisation of police forces, only a part of the central share of the funds should be allotted to the States in cash to meet
their requirements  for improving physical infrastructure such as police stations, etc.  Insofar as weaponry, gadgetry,
equipment, vehicles, etc., the central assistance should always be in kind for the reasons stated in the preceding paragraphs.
 
Delhi Police
 
43.       Policing a city like Delhi is in itself a stupendous task.  Delhi Police has been engaged in this task for long.
However with the passage of every single day its task is becoming more difficult and complex as the population of the city
is growing constantly.  To cope up with the situation, Delhi Police needs updating its strength, technology and
infrastructure.   Keeping in view the need for modernisation as well as the need to enable Delhi Police to meet the emerging
challenges, BPR&D was entrusted with the task of studying manpower requirements and modernisational needs of Delhi
Police. BPR&D in its Report has touched almost every aspect of police functioning.  It has been more than two years since
BPR&D submitted its Study Report.  Unfortunately, its recommendations have not yet been implemented.  The Report is
still moving back and forth between North Block and Indraprastha Estate.  In this entire process, the Study Report, which
has since been accepted in principle by the Ministry of Home Affairs, has become victim of procrastination and
bureaucratic apathy.  Had this not been true, the Ministry would have come up with a definite timeframe and cost estimates
to implement the Report.  Instead, the Ministry is still groping in the dark.  There is clear ambivalence and lack of
enthusiasm in the Ministry of Home Affairs vis-à-vis the implementation of this Report.  In sharp contrast to this, the same
Ministry prepares, with the help of CPMFs, a perspective plan having a definite timeframe and concrete budgetary
proposals for the modernisation and augmentation of CPMFs, seeks the approval of the Cabinet for the plan and sets the
plan in motion.  Not just that, the Ministry is now in the process of finalising a modernisation plan for SSB also, which has
acquired the status of a CPMF of late.  But when it comes to Delhi Police, why there is so much ambivalence in the
approach of the Ministry of Home Affairs?  Instead of taking the onus upon itself for the implementation of the Report, it
either passes the buck on to the BPR&D for not quantifying the expenditure for implementing its recommendations or
drops the ball in the court of Delhi Police by asking it to prioritise its requirements.  Here the question arises as to whether
the quantification of the expenditure to be incurred in implementing its recommendations was included in the terms of
reference given to the BPR&D?  If not, how can the Ministry wash its hands off by saying that BPR&D did not quantify the

expenditure involved?  So far as asking Delhi Police to prioritise its requirements is concerned, there is nothing wrong in
setting priorities.  But at the same time one must not lose sight of the totality of the picture.  While picking the areas which
require urgent attention, the Ministry should remember that it is incumbent upon it to see that the whole is not ignored for
the sake of the parts. 
 
43.1     As desired by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Delhi Police has sent a list of its priorities to the former for its
consideration.  These priorities are as under:

(c)                Procurement of Electronics Surveillance Equipment and unmarked cars for Special Branch;
(d)               Separation of crime investigation and law & order duties by creation of 1426 posts in various ranks to

43.1.1  It is good that the Delhi Police has submitted concrete proposals after working out the costs involved in their
implementation.  It, however, has not indicated any timeframe for their implementation.  Now it is for the Ministry of
Home Affairs to see that proposals are implemented in a time bound manner so as to begin with the implementation of the
recommendations of BPR&D.  This limited implementation of the recommendations of BPR&D, however, does not
condone the piecemeal manner in which the Ministry intends to implement them.  What is more important and of primary
focus for this Committee is the implementation of BPR&D’s Study Report in its totality within a stipulated timeframe and
with necessary budgetary allocations.
 
43.1.2  Therefore, the Committee while reiterating its earlier recommendations in its 73
rd and 88th Reports on Demands for
Grants (2001-02) and (2002-03), respectively, once again exhorts upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to draw a clear cut
time schedule and quantify the expenditure to be incurred for implementing the recommendations of BPR&D contained in
its Study Report on manpower requirements and modernisational needs of Delhi Police.  The Committee is of the opinion
that the Ministry of Home Affairs, after having drawn a definite time schedule and worked out the costs to be involved in
implementing the recommendations, should seek the approval of the Cabinet for necessary budgetary allocations for that
purpose.      
 
43.2     For a city like Delhi which has the distinction of having the largest number of motor vehicles compared to any other
city in the country, management of ever-growing road traffic should receive utmost attention of the Government with a
long-term perspective.  To the contrary, the Government is more keen to focus on short-term measures rather than finding
some long-term solutions to the numerous problems doting Delhi’s traffic scenario.  This Committee, with a view to look
for a proper mechanism for evolving a long-term perspective plan for management of traffic in Delhi, had recommended for
setting up a Unified Traffic Management Authority in its 73
rd Report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) and reiterated it in
its 88th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03).  On both the occasions, the Ministry of Home Affairs had replied that the
recommendation of the Committee was forwarded to the Government of Delhi which, in turn, has stated that under the
existing constitutional scheme of governance for the National Capital Territory, it may not be possible to bring about an
integrated legislation to set up a Unified Traffic Management Authority.  The matter is, however, being examined by the
Government.  Here, the notable fact is that in its two consecutive ATRs, the Ministry has maintained the same position.  In
last three years, it has not been able to wriggle out of the constitutional quandary as to which of the two Governments is
competent to set up this authority.  Is three years’ time too little to solve this so-called puzzle ?  Given the existing scheme
of constitutional relationship between the Government of Delhi and Government of India, the onus of setting up this
authority is on the Ministry of Home Affairs, as Delhi has still not attained full-fledged statehood.  Besides, matters
pertaining to ‘Police’ and ‘Land’ in relation to NCT of Delhi fall within the jurisdiction of Union Government.  Therefore,
the Committee is of the considered view that Ministry of Home affairs should take immediate steps to set up a Unified
Traffic Management Authority for Delhi.
 
43.3     Housing needs of the personnel of Delhi Police is another important area which has been a cause of concern for this
Committee. It has been expressing its deep concern on this issue for the last four years in its 54
th, 59 th, 73 rd and 88 th

Reports on Demands for Grants of Ministry of Home Affairs.  The various recommendations made by it in these reports
failed to bring any perceptible change in the situation.  The satisfaction level of residential accommodation continues to be

remains the biggest bottleneck in improving the satisfaction level.  Therefore, the existing policy of taking up the

infrastructure are available in the colonies developed by agencies like DDA and GDA both in and around Delhi.  Thus,

the regular budgetary allocations earmarked for it. 
 
43.3.1  Keeping this in view, the Committee fully endorses the view that Delhi Police should be allowed to acquire more
and more ready-built-flats in order to raise the satisfaction level in respect of the residential accommodation for its
personnel.  This should be the policy decision to meet not only the present but also the future housing requirements of Delhi
Police.  The success of this measure will, however, hinge on the allocation of requisite funds.  Accordingly, the Committee
strongly feels that the Government should not only allocate Rs.79 crore to enable Delhi Police to purchase 520 odd flats in
Dwarka sub-city of Delhi for the present but it should also make necessary budgetary provisions for further purchase of
flats by Delhi Police.
 
43.4     Traffic scenario of Delhi continues to be as chaotic as it can get with one problem after the other rearing its head. 
The problems are such which cannot and will not submit to solutions which are one time and adhoc in nature.  Consistence
and persistence should be the guiding principles for any enforcement policy.  The adherence to this principle is more
appropriate than elsewhere in a city like Delhi whose roads witness one of the worst kinds of lawlessness.  One such
problem is the use of high decibel pressure horns used mainly by private passenger buses and other commercial vehicles
plying in the city.  Although, Delhi Police takes punitive action against the vehicles fitted with pressure horns, the situation
is far from being under control.  Here, a special mention may be made of the private passenger buses plying under Stage
Carriage Scheme of State Transport Authority which are invariably fitted with pressure horns.  The drivers of these buses
blare pressure horns with impunity and thus cause immense noise pollution which continues unabated.  Interestingly, Delhi
Traffic Police is finding it beyond its means to check the use of pressure horns by a few thousands of buses plying in Delhi. 
Apparently, there is lack of persistence in the enforcement drive to rid the city of these ear deafening horns.  All that is
needed to be done is not being done.  The way the operators of these buses are being allowed to get away with, after
causing immense damage to the health of the people, it appears that some kind of complicity exists between them and
certain levels of Delhi Traffic Police. 
 
43.4.1  Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the situation warrants immediate action on the part of Delhi Traffic
Police to see that Delhites get rid of this menace of pressure horns once and for all.  The Committee recommends that the
Delhi Traffic Police should not only immediately launch a citywide drive against the use of pressure horns especially by
private passenger buses but should also sustain it till such time the city is declared “Free of Pressure Horns”.  It is also of
the view that stringent measures should be taken to prohibit not just the use of pressure horns but also their sale, purchase
and possession within the municipal limits of Delhi.  The Committee would like to take stock of the situation after the lapse
of three months from the date of presentation of its Report in the wake of its above stated recommendation. 
 
Modernisation of Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs)
 
44.       The Central Para Military Forces (CPMFs) have been playing a very crucial role in thwarting both external and
internal threats to the security of the nation.  The vital role being played by them can very well be understood by the fact
that most of these forces are deployed to nearly 100% of their strength which also means that their reserves too are fully
deployed.  This shows how strenuous and difficult is the nature of the duties being performed by the personnel of CPMFs. 
While performing various tasks assigned to them, these forces not only have had to maintain a constant pressure on their

98th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/98threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:57:49]
adversaries such as militants, insurgents, mercenaries, etc. by way of dynamic deployment, they also have to bear in mind
that their weaponry, gadgetry, equipment, etc. are in no way inferior to those of their adversaries.  With a view to enhance
their striking capabilities in terms of better firepower and a fully equipped manpower, the modernisation plans of six
CPMFs, namely, BSF, CRPF, NSG, CISF, ITBP and Assam Rifles have been put underway.  The modernisation plan for
the seventh CPMF i.e. SSB is also under consideration of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  The notable feature of this
modernisation exercise is that it is being carried out as per a comprehensive perspective plan with concrete budgetary
allocations spread over a time frame of five years.  These modernisation plans inter alia aim at augmentation of the
manpower of the CPMFs.  Accordingly, in all 209 battalions have been sanctioned for CPMFs including India Reserve (IR)
Battalions and Rashtriya Rifles.  Out of these 209 battalions, 127 battalions have been sanctioned to be raised during 2000-
01, 2001-02 and 2002-03.  The remaining 82 battalions are proposed to be raised during 2003-04 and 2004-05 at the rate of
41 battalions in each year.  While the battalions/companies sanctioned during   2000-01 and 2001-02 have already been
raised, the battalions sanctioned for 2002-03 are in the process of raising.
 
44.1     This Committee has all along been in favour of strengthening the CPMFs and will continue to support any
measure/proposal aimed at keeping them in tune with changing times in future too.  While the Committee fully endorses the
on-going exercise of modernisation and augmentation of CPMFs, it, however, would tend to draw the attention of the
Ministry of Home Affairs to some of the practical difficulties being faced by the forces in the wake of the implementation
of their modernisation plans.  The Committee is given to understand that most of the newly sanctioned battalions being
raised are, in effect, nothing but addition of a few more companies to the existing battalions.  The net result of this exercise
is that instead of raising new battalions which have their own infrastructure, chain of command, area of operation, etc., the
existing battalions are being stuffed with more personnel without any support paraphernalia.  For instance, 38 companies
have been sanctioned to ITBP to convert its 19 battalions from 4 company pattern to 6 company pattern.  But administration
staff such as cooks, washerman, barber and water carrier, and support staff for telecom, motor transport, animal transport,
dog squad, etc. have not been sanctioned.  The lack of administration and support staff not only renders the additional
companies operationally dysfunctional but also puts extra strain on the already stretched out infrastructure of the existing
battalions.  Therefore, in view of the situation as explained above, the Committee expresses the view that necessary
paraphernalia should be provided to the additional companies being raised as per the modernisation plans of CPMFs.  It is
of the opinion that the very purpose behind modernisation and augmentation plans will be defeated if the additional
battalions/companies are rendered dysfunctional due to lack of necessary support system.
 
44.2     As mentioned elsewhere in this Report, the process of raising 127 battalions out of the total 209 newly sanctioned
battalions of CPMFs including IR battalions and Rashtriya Rifles, is due for completion by the close of the financial year
2002-03.  With the raising of these 127 battalions, it is expected that CPMFs will be able to relieve their reserve battalions
from various areas of operation.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that as soon as these127 battalions are fully
operationalised, the reserve battalions of all CPMFs should be withdrawn from operational duties to the extent possible. 
With the withdrawal of reserve battalions, the Committee hopes that sufficient number of jawans could be spared for
training, etc. so as not only to improve the quality of manpower but also to reduce the stress level of the jawans.
 
44.3     Another closely related aspect of the modernisation and augmentation process of CPMFs is the quality of their
human resource.  While there is no gainsaying the fact that CPMFs need to be modernised and their strength needs
augmentation but at the same time we should not lose sight of the quality of their manpower.  In our attempt to see that our
security forces are not outnumbered by their adversaries, we should not end up raising a huge army of jawans who are not
properly looked after, are not provided with quality diet, clothes, accessories, etc. and are not spared for sufficient relief and
recreation.  In addition, welfare measures are also not compromised.  In the view of the Committee, there is an urgent need
to focus on the well being of the jawans of CPMFs so as to improve their allround development.  Accordingly, it
recommends that the Government should lay equal emphasis on the quality of manpower of CPMFs while making attempts
to augment their quantity.
 
44.4     The living conditions for jawans in the barracks of CPMFs also need mention.  The Committee is given to
understand that the upkeep of the barracks is very poor which has a direct impact on the health and well being of jawans. 
Lack of proper attention, adequate funds, etc. are some of the reasons behind the poor conditions in the barracks.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate funds should be earmarked to improve living conditions in the barracks of
the jawans.  Besides, strict and clear guidelines should be issued to ensure proper upkeep of the barracks.     
 
Housing for CPMFs
 
45.       No other issue than the housing requirements of the personnel of Central Para Military Forces has attracted the
